column2: "West Window Restoration and Protecting the Environment"
column3:
"St Swithun’s Church, situated in Bournemouth’s Town Centre is a vital community resource to the local people. We deliver a wide range of activities to meet local needs and provide for our community. To be able to continue to do this we need to carry out works to the building.

Our West Window, one of the most striking features, is in urgent need of restoration as its condition is rapidly deteriorating. We also have an inadequate heating system that is nearing the end of its life, is expensive to run and has high carbon emissions. 

Window repairs and a new air source heat pump system will see the building protected for the future. In addition, we are exploring our heritage in greater detail to make it more widely known and accessible to visitors as well as teaching people about the importance of environmental sustainability."

"Christchurch Priory seeks to secure its future as a place of worship, community and heritage by undertaking urgent conservation works and laying the groundwork for long-term transformation. This project will repair and sensitively relay the nave floor, addressing serious safety, accessibility, and conservation concerns. Alongside this, a package of specialist audits and assessments will shape the future delivery of the wider Priory Masterplan. Investigations will guide future heating and lighting upgrades, improved access to our collections, and engagement with the Priory's untold stories. We want to better understand how visitors engage with the Priory, and how to remove barriers that exclude people. This project includes business planning, stakeholder consultation, and audience research, to develop a sustainable, inclusive vision that reflects the building’s historic significance and engagement potential. Our goal is to care for the Priory’s fabric, broaden participation, and ensure Christchurch Priory continues to inspire, welcome and serve its community."

The Manchester Prize is a landmark challenge prize that aims to drive pioneering AI innovation by rewarding UK-led breakthroughs in AI for public good.The Round 2 focuses on using AI for Clean Energy Systems. The grants, managed via our delivery partner Nesta, will incentivise development of cutting-edge applications of AI to solve challenges across high-impact domains. The project aims to accelerate and showcase the potential of AI to be used in a way that benefits people, society and supports a community of leading AI for public good innovators in the UK. We anticipate that the project supports the UK governments wider objectives in the following ways:Positioning the UK as a Science and Tech Superpower: The Manchester Prize will accelerate innovation, stimulate investment and help to position the UK as a global leader in AI, supporting the AI Strategy ambition for the UK to cement its position as a science and technology superpower.Stimulating and demonstrating the use of AI for public good, in line with objective 5 of the AI Safety Summit. Solutions developed through the Manchester Prize will showcase socially beneficial UK AI innovation, as the focus of the prize challenge will be AI for Public Good and AI safety and ethics will remain a key judging criterion for the Manchester Prize. The solutions developed by finalist teams will serve as clear examples of the positive potential of AI.Supporting better outcomes for UK Citizens: By incentivising AI development in areas of public importance, like Climate Change, Energy and Environment, the prize aims to generate downstream benefits for UK society. The first round of the Prize has already accelerated the development of key AI solutions relating to areas relating topublic good areas such as energy efficiency, improving public infrastructure, reducing water loss and crop efficiency.Developing a highly skilled community of AI Innovators: The prize will contribute to nurturing the UKs world-leading AI research community, by incentivizing AI development in areas of public importance and bringing together developers, problem-holders, adopters and investors.The challenge is also closely aligned with the government's key missions, in particular, mission 1 (kickstart economic growth) through supporting investment and growth in UK technology startups and organisation and mission 2 (make Britain a clean energy superpower) through its focus on green growth and AI for clean energy systems.

With our work developing the Gaelic Café project over the last 6 years, lessons learned and experience acquired from all of our community events and activities, we feel the time is right to expand the Gaelic culture aspect of the project in order to engage with more of the community. We want to use Gaelic cultural props (see below) to stimulate Gaelic conversation.Our innovative approach of delivering the first part of these monthly sessions in both Gaelic and English broadens cultural awareness and taps into the Gaelic knowledge of the participants, whether or not they have any previous experience of the language. It also offers those who do have some knowledge of the language experience of Gaelic at a high level.This project aims to do two things:1. Provide opportunity for those with a knowledge of the Gaelic language and Gaelic learners to:take part in some authentic Gaelic conversation in order to advance there Gaelic beyond basic biographical conversation about the weekend.practice any Gaelic learnt in order to keep it freshshare Gaelic related experiences and learningincrease the range and level of there vocabulary2. Raise awareness of Gaelic language and the Gàidhealtachd in general both locally and to any visiting the area:our resident community is diverse with many people coming from other parts of the world and from different culturesvisitors to Highland Perthshire are looking to learn something about our culture and heritagemany GME parents have little or no knowledge of the GàidhealtachdThis will be delivered by inviting a speaker along to deliver a relevant topic bi-lingually which will then spark Gaelic conversation at our monthly Gaelic café, which will follow this session.Examples of the Gaelic Culture Props would include:Demonstration/discussion/presentation of :Traditional crafts - perhaps sone from the Red List of Endangered Crafts eg:DyeingSpinningGanseysBlacksmithingTraditional Musiclooking at and listening to tunes - what they mean and what they are calledinstruments - demo/discussion on history and learning names for partsLiteraturelooking at Gaelic PoetryPerthshire Gaelic folktales and songs collected and recorded in 1891 by Lady Evelyn Stewart Murray The EnvironmentPlace names in Highland PerthshireCrofting - the lost words and ways of Crofting

The Project for which I am applying is called Mòd Acadamaidh an Òbain - our aim is to further develop all aspects of the Gaelic language - singing, oral and most importantly we will be encouraging all the children to converse in gaelic - both basic and fluent.Everyone will benefit from this Project as older family members will become interested and then hopefully want to learn to be able and to understand what their children are learning. With this Project we aim to encourage and teach as many Local children as possible, to both sing and converse in Gaelic at every opportunity. The children will definitely benefit from being taught and using Gaelic, most of whom are from non Gaelic Medium Schools and homes.We will be tutoring children from pre-school up to the age of 18 in both gaelic singing and orals. The children will be entering Provincial and National Mods. They will also be singing at Ceilidhs and the Local Care Homes..We hope to achieve an increase in learning, participating and interest in the Gaelic language.

This project is to encourage children to take part in the Local and National Mod. the children are helped to prepare for singing with the choir, and poems, solos, and action songs. They are taught the prescribed songs and other local songs. We hold workshops on a weekly basis, including attending the Gaelic Medium Unit in Salen Primary School.There is very little Gaelic input in the other primary schools in Mull and Iona, so it is important to have outside tuition available to direct children in the use of the Gaelic language, and to encourage them to participate in Mods.The parents of the children involved are eager for them to take part as they recognise that they enjoy singing, and it extends their knowledge of the language and culture, particularly when they are learning songs of their own community. Workshops will be conducted through the medium of Gaelic as far as possible.

This project, Siuthad Gàidhlig!, aims to set up and establish an annual programme of Gaelic language and cultural activities for families throughout Perth and Kinross that will comprise of: Monthly weekend activities for Gaelic learners through the medium of Gaelic. The activities will be different each month, and include a wide variety of sporting, adventurous, creative and cultural activities. School holiday day camp activities for Gaelic learners through the medium of Gaelic. The activities will include a variety of sporting, adventurous, creative and cultural activities. Complementary fun family events, such as ceilidhs and family fun days. The main individuals who will benefit from this project are Gaelic learners throughout Perth and Kinross (principally from Breadalbane Academy primary and secondary school, Goodlyburn Primary School and Perth Academy), and their families. Once established, the activities will also be open to Gaelic learners and their families from outside of the Perth and Kinross area. As well as the many and varied benefits for individuals of participating in each activity, the main aims for providing these sessions for participants is so that they can take their Gaelic outside of the classroom; they can use and develop their language skills in new, exciting and challenging contexts. We hope to establish and sustain a recurring annual programme of activities that allow to go from almost non-existent to de rigeur. This includes both developing activity sessions in the medium of Gaelic and supporting and facilitating the delivery of these sessions through the medium of Gaelic.

A' ceangal Cowal is Comann Nam Pàrant Chòmhghall's project for 2025. Aims: Promote Gaelic language, education and culture in Cowal, where interest is picking up a pace. Increase community confidence in using Gaelic language.Beneficiaries: Children, young people, their families and wider community. 12 children (currently in the Gaelic Early Learning Centre) will join Gaelic Primary 1 in August 2025. A' ceangal Cowal, will provide a cross-generational opportunity to connect with local enthusiasts for Gaelic language and culture - to the benefit of all.A' ceangal Cowal will be made up of various events over the year:Gaelic Homelink Cowal - website update and relaunch: April/May 2025 Relaunch to encourage more engagement with current parents/carers as well as to familiarise those from the incoming GME P1 cohort.Thusa is mise - following / linked to the website relaunch, an intensive 2-day language learning experience for parents/carers of children in GME. Childcare provided in the form of an accompanying age appropriate Gaelic creche with structured Gaelic language activities. This experience will take place in September, once the new term has settled, then be 'topped up' around once per term with less intensive workshops.Còmhla - October holiday 'playscheme': The 'tattie holidays' last a fortnight in Cowal and Còmhla will run during the first week so as not to clash with the Mòd. It will involve P1 - S3 GME pupils in age appropriate activities.Fàilte Immersion Day. An early November stay-and-play event for all families who are pre-nursery / in nursery, intrigued by GME. Nursery staff / teachers in attendance. Gaelic Bookbug session. Free takeaway Gaelic resources and books.

Ceanglan Chaluim Chille, based on the inspiration of Colmcille, will creatively explore Gaelic language within the context of environmental and natural heritage themes. Based on the power of the arts to engage interest, increase confidence and learning, this project will use approaches drawn from visual art, textiles, song lyrics, music, creative writing, to interactively engage with community audiences. Supported by Foras na Gaeilge, based at heritage sites on Mull/Iona, in Campbeltown and Mid-Argyll, the project grows CHARTS Gaelic development to date, improving access to Gaelic conversation and learning. Designed from the outcomes of Cuairt Chaluim Chille, supported by Bòrd na Gàidhlig and Foras na Gaeilge, the project will further development between Argyll and Ireland, through shared environment and climate change themes across borders.Ceanglan Chaluim Chille will develop from three key-event opportunities led by fluent Irish and Scots Gaelic speakers/artists:Phase one (2025) on Mull and Iona, will enable two three-day residencies, for one Ireland and one Argyll based practitioner, to separately lead Gaelic language workshop-events using heritage themes and art, engaging with community and youth groups. Activities will take place on Mull at Aros Walled Garden and KNOCKvologan, a residency hub for art, literature and research, and on Iona. Day and evening activities will be led in Gaelic and translated to English.Phase two (2026), based at Campbeltown and Kilmartin Museums will build on phase one outcomes to increase participation, including walks in Kilmartin Glen. One residency will be created for Argyll based practitioner/s to further explore Colmcille and local environmental heritage.The project will include participation from CHARTS Gaelic Officer, Gaelic members (including horticulture/arts) and heritage-staff.

column3: Aon Ghuth Gaelic Makaton Choir was established by myself as a side project of a charity called F.A.I.R - Fairness, Acceptance, Inclusion, Respect in April 2024.The aim of the project was to make Gaelic language & culture more accessible to people with additional support & communication needs; to raise awareness of & promote Makaton & the power of inclusion; to foster new experiences & opportunities especially for those who feel isolated from their local communities. Our mission was for the choir to perform & be included in The Royal National Mod in Oban last year.Aon Ghuth made their debut performance at Ar Canan' s Ar Ceol - a concert organised by Sileas Sinclair to mark the opening of the Royal National Mod in Oban In October 2024. Our performance was very warmly received & the feedback we've had has been so positive & heartwarming.The main beneficiaries of Aon Ghuth are the choir members, the local & wider communities of both Gaelic & non Gaelic speakers, users of Makaton.We want to take Aon Ghuth to a wider audience both locally & further afield, inspiring more people to become involved with Gaelic & Makaton. column2: Gàidhlig anns a’ chruth-thìre Pheairt is Cheann Rois – Gaelic in the landscape of Perth & Kinross
column3: Perth & Kinross is an area that is rich in Gaelic heritage, and there is clear evidence of this throughout the landscape in the names of hills, glens and water courses. Hill walkers are often aware of the Gaelic names but most find them more of a hindrance than a help because they can’t pronounce them, while people who don’t often open an OS map can be completely unaware of the Gaelic in plain sight all around them and often assume that Gaelic was never spoken this far south. Through carefully planned half-day, low-level hill walks, we aim to illuminate the Gaelic landscape of the Perthshire hills, explain the meanings of the Gaelic names all around, and explore some of the local legends and folklore, as well as talking about how widely Gaelic was spoken in Perth & Kinross and explaining how and when its use declined in the area. We believe strongly that Gaelic and the landscape are natural partners, and we hope to show people how deeply Gaelic is rooted in our landscape and open up for participants that extra dimension of understanding that comes when you realise that the names actually mean something. We will also take the opportunity of several hours walking in nature to build connections and to chat to participants on an individual basis about Gaelic learning opportunities in Perth & Kinross and about the value of Gaelic as an economic asset to the region. As a final output from this project, we intend to document the walks with photographs and written information, with the aim of generating a digital trail that independent hill walkers can follow without a human guide. This is part of a longer term aspiration to create a Gaelic Heritage Trail in Perth & Kinross.

column3: This project will deliver regular in-person Gaelic conversation opportunities in Perth & Kinross to give Gaelic learners the chance to develop their spoken Gaelic and use the Gaelic they have been learning, and to use it in a more natural and social settings.Being able to speak Gaelic is the most difficult part of learning and is normally the last skill to develop for adult learners. Many learners are extremely competent at reading and even writing in Gaelic but are likely to struggle with listening and speaking skills, particularly in an area like Perth & Kinross, where Gaelic is not spoken as a community language. Even advanced learners who are capable of holding a decent conversation become rusty through lack of opportunity to chat with others and extend their vocabulary. There are 3 aspects to this project: Providing guided conversation sessions for post beginner and intermediate learners; providing less formal conversation-café type opportunities for advanced learners and fluent speakers; providing very informal social events for learners of any level to come together to speak/sing in Gaelic. Guiding the newer learners requires a fair amount of advance preparation by a competent Gaelic speaker who can develop suitable topics and questions and help the learners to find ways to express themselves with the vocabulary they know as well as assisting them with new vocabulary. This is a big ask of a volunteer, and we feel that it would be a good test of change to see if a group or groups like this could form part of a sustainable model in Perth & Kinross. To ensure that we can provide a regular offering, we would like to engage a leader or leaders to direct and run these sessions on a paid basis rather than rely on volunteers. More advanced learners don’t normally require as much guidance, but it is still desirable to have a competent Gaelic speaker on hand to steer the conversation and encourage shyer, less fluent and new participants to join in. We hope to recruit leaders who will donate their time to help on a rota basis with such groups, but we feel that while it is reasonable to ask them to volunteer their time, they shouldn’t be out of pocket with regard to travelling expenses, particularly as Perth & Kinross is a very large geographical area, and we would hope to run these sessions in public places such as cafes throughout the area. The third aspect of the project is very informal ‘pop-up Gàidhealtachd’ type social events to include learners and speakers of all levels from throughout Tayside. These sessions would be held in public places such as pubs, but again would benefit from a sort of ‘fear an taighe’ (host) role to help new people to feel part of the group, to promote conversation, and to encourage everyone to join in, as well as a musician/singer who would be prepared to take the lead in encouraging people to sing or play, as this is an important part of Gaelic culture, and one which we aim to encourage in Perth & Kinross. Again, we would like to be able to offer these helpers travelling expenses (if they wished to claim these), as some may have a fair distance to travel.

column3: Ti agus Puirt Peairt will extend our highly successful Tea and Tunes project model which was initially piloted in Kirkcaldy, Fife in 2022 and subsequently replicated in Gaelic in partnership with the Caird Hall in Dundee. Both series now run regularly on an annual basis. Presenting this project in Perth will extend our reach and be part of Live Music Now Scotland’s national programme for music and older people. Ti agus Puirt Peairt is designed to bring older people together through music and socialising, targeted especially for people living in social isolation and/or living with dementia, either as carer or personally. Audiences will be able to experience the best of Scotland’s emerging Gaelic singers and instrumentalists in a secure and comfortable environment, bringing older and younger generations together through interactive music-making and social interaction, including in Gaelic, with each other over a cup of tea and home-baking. Performances are in daylight hours, enabling the audience to travel by public or community transport and without the anxiety of being out on dark evenings. Financial barriers are removed through free and open access to all and inviting a non-obligatory donation. We will work in partnership with St Ninian’s Cathedral (Perth Cathedral), South Methven Street, Perth in promoting two series of four afternoon performances each year for two years, a total of 16 performances showcasing Gaelic artists. Musicians, who are all auditioned and trained, will be from Live Music Now Scotland’s roster of Gaelic artists.

column3: Tha an tagradh seo airson maoineachadh fhaotainn gus sreath den leasanan Gàidhlig a lìbhrigeadh do luchd-ionnsachaidh agus gus cearcall-còmhraidh a chumail do luchd-labhairt na Gàidhlig aig a bheil ìre eadar-mheadhanach agus air adhart ann am Meadhan Earra-Ghàidheal. A rèir an rannsachaidh a chaidh a dhèanamh o chionn ghoirid, tha an t-uabhas dhaoine ann am meadhan Earra-Ghàidheal ag iarraidh leasanan aghaidh ri aghaidh ag amas air luchd-tòiseachaidh. Agus a bharrachd air sin, tha goireas a dhìth air a’ choimhearsnachd do luchd-ionnsachaidh no luchd-labhairt aig a bheil tuigse air a’ chànan no comas air còmhradh a chumail airson Gàidhlig a bhruidhinn is a chleachdadh aig an ìre freagarrach dhaibh gus adhartas a dhèanamh. Tron chearcall-còmhraidh seo, bidh mi ag amas air brosnachadh agus misneachd a thoirt do na daoine a bhios an làthair le geamannan, gnìomhan agus taic a thaobh puingean cànain.’S mar sin, le taic is aonta bhon bhuidheann ionadail aithnichte de luchd-ionnsachaidh na Gàidhlig, an canar ris Companaich Dhail Riada, tha mi a’ cur a-steach airson taic-airgid mar neach fa leth gus am feum agus an t-iarrtas seo a choileanadh. Ma shoirbhicheas leis an tagradh seo agus an iomairt seo a thèid a thoirt seachad leam fhìn, beachdaichidh Companaich Dhail Riada air tagradh a chur a-steach mun àm seo an-ath-bhliadhna gus togail air an adhartas a thèid a dhèanamh mar thoradh air an t-sreath de chlasaichean agus cearcall-còmhraidh a lìbhrigeas mi don choimhearsnachd. A thaobh structar nan clasaichean do luchd-tòiseachaidh, tha dùil agam ris na goireasan SpeakGaelic A1 ùisneachadh gus dèanamh cinnteach gun tèid adhartas a dhèanamh am measg nan oileanach. Agus a bharrachd air sin, cuiridh mi ris na clasaichean leis na stuthan ionnsachaidh eile agam agus bheir mi an cothrom dhaibh eòlas a chur air dualchainnt na sgìre. Thathar an dòchas gum bi an iomairt seo na bhuannachd do dhaoine de gach seòrsa air feadh na sgìre a chionn ’s gun toir e cothrom air leth is ruigsinneach do mhuinntir na sgìre gus Gàidhlig ionnsachadh nach eil ri fhaighinn san sgìre seo an ceartair agus nach eil air a bhith ri fhaighinn o chionn fhada.

column2: Dàimh na Tìre: Gaelic Heritage, Community, and the Future of the Land
column3: Dàimh na Tìre: Gaelic Heritage, Community, and the Future of the Land is a 24-month intergenerational project dedicated to actively encouraging, supporting, and facilitating the sustained use of Gaelic among families in Perthshire.This £10,000 request from the Bòrd na Gàidhlig is strategically allocated to fund the project's core Gaelic delivery and educational infrastructure. This includes £6,000 for a specialist Gaelic Workshop Facilitator to lead ten Gaelic-medium workshops across five partner schools, plus associated travel and administration costs (£1,100). The workshops are the fieldwork phase, structured to move Gaelic usage beyond the classroom and into practical, real-world contexts like environmental stewardship and traditional food knowledge.The grant further enables crucial intergenerational knowledge transfer by providing funds to compensate at least eight Gaelic Knowledge Holders (£500) and supporting the Junior Heritage/Recipe Tester Honorarium (£400). This ensures the knowledge collected is authentic, respectful, and tested for practical use. A portion of the funding (£600) also contributes to specialist Ecological/Gaelic Consultancy to validate the resource’s accuracy.Crucially, the book's content is designed to be the foundational curriculum for our new Family Forest School (launching late 2026). The Bòrd's funding for content creation ensures this permanent community asset will continue to enable and stimulate Gaelic usage among families long after the project concludes. Finally, the grant covers £1,400 for launch and dissemination, ensuring the resource reaches the target Gaelic audience.

column2: "Cultural Glenkens – Preserving the heritage of our place."
column3:
"Our natural heritage is of key importance to us here in the Glenkens in remote-rural SW Scotland. We are situated in a UNESCO Biosphere due to the uniqueness of our landscapes, yet they are changing very rapidly. 
Our cultural heritage is also highly valued. From the Covenanters to the Galloway Hoard to 20th century rural living, our heritage is celebrated and revered – but is at risk from volunteer fatigue and the passage of time. 
At the Glenkens Community and Arts Trust, we have a 17-year track record of weaving together Arts, Community and Heritage so that people can better connect to the heritage of the Glenkens. Through ‘Cultural Glenkens’ we want to amplify the work of our amazing volunteers, catalyse new engagement projects and better record our heritage. We also want to support our young people through a programme of internships, supporting the sustainability of our modern rural community."

column3:
"The Solway Firth is one of the most important estuaries in Britain, shared between Scotland and England, its amazing seascape is vital for people and wildlife. The Dumfries and Galloway coastline runs for 210 miles from the shimmering sands of the inner Solway to the rugged shores of Wigtownshire, and the Mull of Galloway, Scotland’s most southerly point. The Firth has shaped the history, economy, art and culture of Scotland, a gateway to the world and a rich natural resource, however its diverse habitats are fragmented and inaccessible. 

SCAMP will address this decline by harnessing Solway’s natural capital to respond to the climate & nature crises, by reconnecting habitats, creating resilient communities and boosting local economic activity. Coastal communities will be at the heart of this holistic seascape approach, and we will focus our work on five key habitats: native oyster reefs, seagrass beds, saltmarsh, sand dunes and coastal woodlands."

column2: "Leadership Labs - A Leadership Training Programme for Senior Climate and Environmental Leaders in Scotland"
column3:
"As we enter the final half of this crucially important decade for climate and nature action, ‘supporting those that do environmental work to be more effective’ is an increasingly critical pillar of EFN's work.

Through strategically partnering with I.G. Advisors (I.G.) – impact strategy experts – we’ll pilot delivering bespoke leadership training to 60 senior leaders of small and medium sized organisations who need it most in the climate, environment and natural heritage space across Scotland.

Leaders will gain renewed enthusiasm, confidence, practical skills and new connections to further boost their leadership, improve the sustainability of their organisations, and catalyse their essential work supporting nature recovery and environmental sustainability of our natural heritage to ensure this remains accessible for communities to enjoy in years to come.

To ensure long-term impact, EFN will provide ongoing support for trained leaders through our Green Fundraisers Forum and other meetings, events and resources."

"We would like to upgrade our Grade B Listed church so that it can be more widely used by the community and be more comfortable for the congregation and all others who use the building. By making the building improvements we believe we will enhance the economic viability of the building and ensure it survives for future generations to enjoy for many years to come. The building is located in the centre of the Royal Burgh of Kirkcudbright, population 3,500, whose charter dates back to 15th century. We have split the redevelopment into two phases. Phase 1 will include the provision of accessible toilets and a tea/coffee servery area, a more welcoming entrance area, improved heating and lighting and a glass partition separating this area from the rest of the church. The legacy of the project will be a building, fit for purpose, for both congregation and community."

"During FIRNS1, we explored the potential for a catchment-scale network of river restoration works on the River Annan, and how the community could be engaged in the project.

During FIRNS2, we began putting these findings into practice, taking a learning by doing approach to getting the process running piloting site development and community events.

In FIRNS3, we would take what we have learned and delivered in the upper-catchment and to expand this considerably throughout the mid and lower catchments. This would achieve catchment-scale coverage, and allow us to put the process developed in FIRNS2 into action.

This will increase reach of the project, and its value to a greater diversity of funders.

We will also work closely with interested local contractors and businesses to build skills and expertise required to deliver restoration works are increasingly available within the local area, and that investment is shared amongst local communities and businesses."

column2: "Transform: a new vision for the collection gallery"
column3: "‘Transform: a new vision for the collection gallery’ is a bold move to rethink the Design Museum’s collection and its display at a time of global societal, political and climate change. An expanded collection gallery will engage a wider public in the story of the impact of design – which helped to shape the 20th century as a creative discipline largely focused on commercial productivity. We now see design emerging as a tool to engage critically with the world, central in tackling climate change, pollution, deforestation, species extinction and the displacement of people. These themes, alongside a strong focus on broad representation and inclusion, will be explored in public through reframing our collection of largely industrially produced objects. New themes, perspectives and voices will provide new interpretations of our shared design heritage for future generations, inviting audiences to interrogate world views and preconceptions, as well as who and what is presented."

column3:
"Restore and protect Perth’s oldest building, the A-listed St. John’s Kirk, ensuring it is wind and watertight. Repairs include asphalt roofs and the 15th-century leaded-broach spire, enabling tours to the bells and tower with stunning views. Improved access will allow people with mobility issues main-entrance access for the first time.

Visitors to St. John’s will enjoy a modern visitor experience that is inclusive, educational and inspirational. The historic site will offer improved interpretation, learning opportunities, and diverse cultural and heritage events. The project will catalyse a new vision for St. John’s as a hub for worship, alongside varied arts and culture, tourism, community, and heritage programmes.

Community engagement and education play a key role. Skilled conservation tradespeople – stonemasons, lead workers, and woodworkers – will undertake the work, with skills development opportunities for young people to gain sector experience. Plans have been designed to support environmental improvements, organisational sustainability and economic growth."
column11: National Lottery Heritage Grants £250,000 to £10 million
column14: St Johns Kirk of Perth Trust

column2: "Urgent Remedial work on the Old Corn Mill, Bunessan"
column3: "This project is to fund urgent emergency remedial work on the walls of the 18th century corn mill in Bunessan, Isle of Mull, so that the structure is secure and safe for visitors to enter. In addition it will fund interpretation boards for the inside and outside of the mill explaining the history and how the mill functioned so that visitors, both local and from away, might understand and appreciate more about this important piece of local heritage. Carrying out these repairs will preserve the structure in the long term, supporting potential redevelopment in the future as a community asset, if and when the community wishes."

column2: "Restoration of the 13th century Choir of Dunkeld Cathedral"
column3:
"Through repair, restoration and development, this project will ensure that the 13th century Choir of Dunkeld Cathedral is preserved for generations to come.   

We aim to ensure that the building can continue to be safely accessed and used by the local congregation and community, and the many national and international visitors who come to Dunkeld every year.   

By improving the interpretation information available, the visitor experience will be enhanced and the story of the Cathedral’s place in the history of Scotland will be better understood, resulting in visitors spending longer at the site which in turn will benefit the local economy.

Improving the current heating and lighting systems to be more environmentally sustainable, and upgrading the audio/visual services will allow the building to be used year-round both as a place of worship and as a venue for concerts and events."
column11: National Lottery Heritage Grants £250,000 to £10 million
column14: The Parish of Dunkeld Church of Scotland

column3:
"Sustaining VIC32: Scotland’s Last Sailing Clyde Puffer

VIC32 is the UK’s only remaining steam-powered Clyde Puffer still sailing, offering weeklong passenger holidays on Scotland’s West Coast, River Clyde, Caledonian and Crinan Canals. This project ensures continued preservation, financial viability, and sustainability.

Works include completing hull plating, rebuilding the wooden wheelhouse, asbestos removal and engineering overhauls to the steam engine condenser, and propeller shaft.

To reduce emissions and costs, VIC32 will transition to biofuel, install a waste oil recovery system, add a foresail and fit a steam turbine generator.

The project will provide specialist, hands-on maritime and steam engineering training for crew, apprentices, and passengers, while expanding access to a more inclusive and diverse visitor base.

A new community and education space at Crinan will support volunteer and training activities. 

Strengthening the trustee board and involving more Scottish people across the project will help secure VIC32’s future for generations to come."

"Through a series of creative, educational and social heritage-based activities, the project aims to: 

- Preserve the heritage and stories associated with The Stoll Foundation as they face risks due to our upcoming move.  

- Improve the wellbeing of our beneficiaries during a turbulent time, while teaching key heritage skills and providing new opportunities. 

- Create a sense of place at our new-build development by exploring the lost and forgotten heritage of the area and easing the transition of the move.  

- Build lasting connections with the local community (civilian and veteran) while increasing awareness of veterans’ issues and The Stoll Foundation’s work and history.  

The project will create permanent ties between our old and new sites as well as our residents and local communities. It will generate renewed interest in The Stoll Foundation’s mission and will preserve both tangible and intangible aspects of our rich heritage for future generations."

"We want to reinvigorate the Trust's purpose, structure and operations, and explore the potential to move the archive into new premises to create a lively heritage centre which would ultimately become a cornerstone of community cohesion, wellbeing and the local economy. 
Liaison with residents/partners will help us create a Collections Development Policy to better reflect local priorities, new outreach work with the community will explore how our work could enhance people's everyday lives, and work with hospitality providers will investigate options for joint events/activities. We will understand the skills needed to take our operations to the level expected of the country's best museums, and have in place a robust Forward Plan and income generation strategy to sustain our long term development. Our plans will be shaped by a forthcoming (pre-project), high-profile Festival of Regenerative Tourism - balancing the needs of the visitor economy with those of the locals."

"In the midst of a planetary emergency, the Natural History Museum (NHM)  will use its expertise to support museums across the UK to make their grounds greener, richer and healthier places for everyone to enjoy. 
Innovative mapping technologies will enable museums to showcase what their site offers for nature and for people and use evidence to identify opportunities for enhancement and nature recovery. 
Through a peer support network and skills programme, we will equip museums with the knowledge and confidence to take nature-positive actions on their sites. Embedded throughout will be a commitment to local decision-making and community collaboration. Through collective action with the people who live and work in our communities, we will foster a greater sense of pride and ownership in local green spaces and inspire action towards a more hopeful future."

"‘Boo, Who?’ is a creative heritage project from Life’s a Pitch Projects, celebrating the stories, memories and cultural traditions of LGBTQ+ football fans. In partnership with Chelsea FC, Chelsea Pride, the National Football Museum and others, we'll collect 15 oral histories, host creative “Object Lab” sessions using personal memorabilia, stage archive photography days, and co-create new inclusive football chants rooted in lived experience.

The project responds to the enduring use of the homophobic chant “Chelsea Rent Boy” – using it as a provocation to spark conversation, reclaim narrative, and imagine alternatives that reflect pride, care and visibility. Activities include matchday activations, songwriting workshops, and an Education Day at Stamford Bridge.

Heritage materials will be preserved in a co-created digital archive and shared alongside a free inclusion toolkit for clubs/communities. Our goal is to embed care, creativity and community authorship into football heritage – and show football’s history belongs to all."

column2: "#LC Loch Lomond & The Trossachs Landscape Connections: Restoring our Woodland Mosaic"
column3:
"Across Loch Lomond & The Trossachs National Park there is a shared vision for a resilient living network where nature and people thrive.?However, whilst our natural heritage inspires people worldwide, even here, nature is under threat.? 

Our Landscape Connections Initiative will restore the globally threatened and culturally iconic woodland mosaic at the heart of the National Park. Temperate rainforest, montane scrub, ancient pinewoods and cultural woodlands form one of the most biodiverse landscapes in the UK.?? 

Within an hour for 50% of Scotland’s population, our new restoration zone will protect and enhance this woodland mosaic and connect it to a wider more resilient nature network covering half the Park’s area.? 

Central to this Initiative will be more empowered communities, landowners, businesses and visitors sharing nature restoration benefits and ensuring a healthy future for our species and habitats, and a lasting legacy of skills, training, jobs and inspiring experiences."
column14: Loch Lomond & The Trossachs National Park Authority

column2: "#HP Barking & Dagenham - A Place to be Proud of"
column3:
"Barking & Dagenham – A Place to be Proud of will strengthen the Council’s capacity to work meaningfully with local communities and heritage stakeholders, developing an embedded Culture and Heritage Action Plan informed by their insight and contributions to realise a shared vision, building on our Culture and Heritage Strategy 2025-2030. As part of this process, we will audit the borough’s physical, natural and intangible heritage assets, mapping where heritage can drive pride, participation and place-based renewal.
The project will trial new approaches to widening access, developing infrastructures that enable genuine community agency and ownership through a shared enterprise model rooted in local identity. Using an asset-based, ground-up commissioning approach, it will establish the conditions for a sustainable model of community-led stewardship. The legacy will be a resilient local ecosystem where heritage is co-produced, understood and equitably valued — informing future strategies and investment."
column14: London Borough of Barking and Dagenham

column2: "Lighting up the Hynish Shore Station - Anchoring Heritage, Building Resilience"
column3:
"In 2025, the Tiree community became proud custodians of Scotland’s only community-owned lighthouse shore station. This landmark transfer birthed the Hynish Trust, a SCIO dedicated to transforming the historic Skerryvore Shorestation site into a vibrant hub of heritage, creativity, and resilience—by the community, for the community.
For two years, volunteers have tirelessly driven progress—reviving infrastructure, strengthening governance, and changing the use of buildings to match the Vision. A strong foundation has been laid, however a team is now critical to the future success. The first step is to recruit two essential roles—Heritage Preservation Officer and Sustainability Development Officer—to lead the next phase: embedding heritage into everyday life, celebrating Tiree’s Gaelic-speaking legacy, and unlocking the site’s full potential as a beacon of inclusive growth.
This is a once-in-a-generation opportunity to secure the future of a nationally significant heritage site."

"Appin Rainforest Regeneration Project will promote and support regeneration of Appin’s significant rainforest remnants. The project has two strands: the removal of invasive non-native species (INNS) across c.11,000 ha. (85% of the Appin Community Council area); and work with local landowners to deliver improved herbivore management, focusing particularly on deer control. This landscape-scale project builds upon work previously undertaken to control invasive rhododendron in Glen Creran, a project that has been used as an exemplar for community-based rainforest regeneration. The present Phase 1 Delivery Project expands the scope and scale of previous work, with landowners and the wider community working collaboratively across the whole of the Phase 1 area. The project has been developed by Appin Community Development Trust and its delivery mechanism is designed to generate a mix of sustainable economic and social benefits for the local community in addition to regenerating environmental heritage that is of international significance."

column2: "Cold water heating the Museum of Lead Mining!"
column3:
"We aim to install a heating system which will significantly reduce both the museum's carbon footprint and reliance on electricity, improve financial resilience and provide a template for other rural community buildings.
This project builds on the use of water as a source of energy in the local lead mining industry over the centuries. Working with Edinburgh University, an innovative, water-source, heat exchange system has been developed which will provide hot water and heat the Visitor Centre with energy from the cold water of the burn.  The burn receives water from the old mines at a temperature of 8 degreesC. A field study has demonstrated its effectiveness. There has been no effective heating system since 2021. The new system will provide a more comfortable environment for visitors and staff, as well as better conditions for collection care. This is an opportunity to share this science with the local community."

column2: "Convalescent Coast: Rest, Revival and Resilience. Exploring and activating Dunoon's Victorian heritage"
column3: "Through delivering this project, we will use Dunoon's Victorian heritage to spark meaningful conversations about health, economy and environment in our community today. By uncovering the stories of health reformers, tourism pioneers and soft drink producers, we will create new resources and experiences that connect people with the places and ideas that shaped this coastal town. Through participatory research, co-designed interpretation and heritage-inspired product development, we will engage diverse audiences with intangible heritage that risks being lost. Our vision will build a more connected, resilient community where local heritage organisations work collaboratively, where residents and visitors engage meaningfully with place, and where heritage becomes a catalyst for sustainable economic development. We will demonstrate how small, rural towns can use their distinctive stories to build inclusive wellbeing economies. Ultimately, we envision Convalescent Coast as heritage-led community development, activating heritage to respond to challenges facing Scotland's coastal communities today."

column2: "Our Hidden River: The Story of the Westbourne"
column3:
"The River Westbourne originates in Hampstead Heath, flowing south through Paddington and Knightsbridge before joining the River Thames near Chelsea Bridge. Historically, the Westbourne provided drinking water for Londoners and fed spas, fishponds, and ornamental lakes, including the Serpentine Lake in Hyde Park. About 170 years ago, like many of the lost rivers, it was forced underground as London expanded, becoming part of the city’s urban drainage and sewer system.

With the support of key heritage organisations, we aim to engage community and primary school groups and residents in exploring and sharing the heritage of the River Westbourne, uncovering what London was like when the river ran above ground. We will achieve this through guided walks, research sessions, art workshops, heritage visits, and environmental action.

At the project’s conclusion, we plan to create a leaflet, walking trails, digital resources, community artworks, and a podcast series, informed by participants."

column2: "From Oar to Easel: Walter Greaves and the Making of Modern Chelsea"
column3:
"From Oar to Easel aims to reconnect children, families and the wider community with Chelsea’s lost riverside world through the life and art of Walter Greaves. The project will help a new generation understand how the Thames, the environment and the local community were transformed by engineering, industry and social change. We want to use Greaves’ unique perspective as a waterman-artist to inspire curiosity, creativity and environmental awareness in 400 pupils and the wider community across Westminster and Kensington & Chelsea.
The project will also strengthen local heritage infrastructure by creating long-lasting resources, a KS2 storybook, a documentary film, animations, a public mural and a portable exhibition and three public exhibitions at Chelsea Library. Through inclusive creative work with autistic young people, volunteers and schools, the project will broaden participation in heritage and ensure Greaves’ story becomes accessible, relevant and valued by the communities who live where he once painted."
column14: Royal Borough of Kensington and Chelsea

column2: "160 Years of VisionPK: Stories of Sight, Sound and Community"
column3:
"The project will celebrate VisionPK’s 160th anniversary by preserving and sharing the charity’s rich heritage. The project will research, collect, and digitise historic documents, photographs, and records, protecting fragile materials and making them accessible to the public.

A timeline of VisionPK’s 160-year journey will highlight key milestones, showing how services and support have evolved. An audio wall will capture memories and stories from service users, families, volunteers, and staff through oral history interviews and storytelling workshops, ensuring lived experiences are recorded.

These elements will contribute to a heritage film and be displayed in a heritage exhibition, allowing visitors to explore archives, listen to stories, and engage with the organisation’s history. The film and digital archive will also be shared via screenings, partner organisations, and online platforms.

This project will safeguard VisionPK’s heritage, strengthen community connections, and inspire future generations to value 160 years of stories, support, and impact."
column14: Perth & Kinross Society For The Blind

column3:
"The local community own Stronafian forest which lies upon the hill slopes of Glendaruel. They want to take the lead in understanding the historical assets  they now care for within the forest, for themselves and for visitors to the sites.  

These historical assets  include two main sites:  Firstly, Auchategan which has been inhabited for at least six  periods from early Neolithic to  the 18th century;  Secondly, the nearby chambered cairn of Lephinkil, which was built over hundreds of years within Neolithic times.  At both sites, all that remains are mounds of turf, stones, and slabs.  Although we have some idea of what lies beneath the ground from past excavations and investigations, it is difficult for us to imagine  the structures our predecessors used and how these supported their daily lives compared to ours.

This project aims to provide digital visualisation interpretation of the two sites which is accessible to all."

column2: "Beyond Tourism : From Interpretation to Intervention - Repositioning Whithorn as a Traditional Skills and Climate Hub"
column3: "We propose two-year exploratory project which seeks to reposition Whithorn as a nationally distinctive centre for skills training, rooted in our archaeological collection, demonstrating 1600 years of making with traditional construction skills, and a heritage of sustainable buildings and travel. It will be delivered through a strong partnership model, building on existing delivery of these skills and planned or existing assets. The core innovation is the transformation of the museum and our townscape from primarily interpretative assets, which visitors view, into a living skills campus, offering courses which directly benefit the young, community and visitors. This is a coherent, replicable model for museum-led skills innovation in rural contexts, responding to both local and national priorities for scarce archaeological and heritage construction skills, climate change, demand for different visitor experiences, livelihoods for local people (especially young people), and inclusive growth, while addressing the resilience challenges faced by our rurally remote museum."

column2: "HELPING COMMUNITIES LIVE-WELL – ONE HUNDRED YEARS OF HERITAGE"
column3:
"As we approach 100years of extraordinary community heritage, celebrating our 2029 centenary, we will create rich heritage experiences for 365,000+ visitors across 3years including 65,000+ additional visitors. 
Kingsley Hall will become a recognised centre of accessible heritage, from our vibrant community setting, 7days a week. 
A full programme of community, volunteer led heritage activities will protect, preserve and showcase our heritage, creating new collections and displays, providing enjoyable inspirational heritage learning for many years to come. 
Through harvesting heritage from lived experiences, our heritage storytelling, will enable a people movement of live-well communities. 
We will create Centenary Edition, Legacy Learning Resources for sharing, including a Heritage Community Engagement Toolkit, Board game, Inspiration Cards and Merchandise.  These will become a treasury of community learning resources, for sharing, scaling and adapting for 100’s of communities, regionally and nationally to live-well. Our growth positioning will ensure future sustainability of our heritage for generations."
column14: Kingsley Hall Church And Community Centre

column3:
"We hope to achieve restoration of what may be the rarest pipe-organ in England: the only known UK example by Hippolyte Loret, originally installed in Paris in 1861 and later rescued and brought to Hammersmith during a dramatic effort to protect the possessions of a religious community. Alongside conserving this extraordinary instrument, the project will open up greater public access to its Grade II* state-school site, revealing its remarkable hidden history of women, royalty, subterfuge, escape and resistance.

Its legacy will be to break down the barriers that still obscure this heritage, inspire wider appreciation of pipe-organs and organ music, and create new opportunities for concerts, education and performance. Through engagement with the public, local schools and 1200 students on-site, organ lessons and choral traditions will be revived for future generations, while the project will also strengthen organ-building expertise and support the long-term conservation of the site’s wider heritage assets."

column2: "#HP_ROOTS&FRUITS - unearthing, sharing and celebrating the diverse rural heritage of Barking and Dagenham"
column3:
"ROOTS&FRUITS (R&F), delivered in by Company Drinks in collaboration with diverse communities, in London Borough of Barking and Dagenham (LBBD), will research, preserve, and celebrate the borough's rich rural, land-based, agricultural heritage. 

Through structured, intergenerational activities, underserved communities will uncover, learn, share, and document land stewardship, food growing, harvesting, and rural traditions, often absent from local heritage narratives.

Residents will develop pride in their heritage through community researcher vocational training, skills development, workshops, field trips, exhibitions and harvest celebrations. 

The programme reconnects residents, including young people aged 6–18, with sustainable land-based traditions, strengthening relationships with nature.

R&F enables Company Drinks to embed community heritage across its wider programme, building capacity and testing approaches that support long-term community heritage work in LBBD.

The project has been developed through a year-long consultation with local stakeholders/partners, including Valence House Archives, Women’s Museum, Heritage Rangers, Myvillages, Museum of London, and the Community Economies Institute."

"One Story, Our Voice (OSOV) will explore, uncover and share our community’s inspiring 50 years of history in London: shaped by migrations of early arrivals (fleeing war and unrest), persistence (struggles/establishing new lives, additional arrivals), and growth (now embedded & established – and able to look back!)   

Project Goals:
A) Collecting/archiving/sharing oral histories from British Somalis; esp. first-generation migrants and community leaders, capturing stories of struggle and success.
 B) Engaging local Somali young people (20 participants), through training in oral history, research and storytelling, creating pathways for participant-led heritage work.
 C) Heritage outputs (documentary, digital exhibition, webpage, booklet, podcasts) that transform stories into accessible/modern formats, ensuring reach to wider audiences beyond the immediate community.

Legacy: Somali heritage better represented within local/national contexts, accessible to future generations and researchers. Foundation laid for further work; reinterpretation through galleries, exhibition within Newham Heritage Service/Migration Museum spaces, and other activities that revitalises this heritage."

column2: "Securing the long-term future of Kilmartin Museum"
column3:
"Kilmartin Museum seeks to strengthen its long-term resilience in order to continue researching, conserving and sharing the internationally significant archaeology and natural heritage of Kilmartin Glen. This project will provide the stability needed to develop and implement new income-generating initiatives, helping the museum adapt to current economic challenges while reducing financial vulnerability.
Through this investment, the museum will safeguard the expertise, collections and learning opportunities that have served local communities and visitors for more than 30 years. The project will enable the team to continue uncovering new insights into the lives of Scotland's earliest communities and to share these stories through exhibitions, events, learning programmes and digital engagement.
The legacy of the project will be a stronger, more sustainable museum that can continue to protect and interpret Kilmartin Glen's heritage for future generations, ensuring this internationally important landscape remains accessible, relevant and inspiring to diverse audiences."

"Through this ambitious programme the Natural History Museum will reopen full public access to the Western Wing of the Grade I listed Waterhouse Building - conserving historic fabric, returning two long-closed galleries to public use and redisplaying the Dinosaur Gallery - to create a world-class suite of interconnected galleries exploring life on earth and our relationship with the natural world, helping to grow visitors from 7m to 8m a year. 

The project is at the heart of NHM150, our programme of transformation ahead of our 150th anniversary in 2031, and central to our mission to create advocates for the planet. The three galleries will help visitors understand evolution, biodiversity and ecological change - the foundational concepts needed to engage with the planetary emergency - while a nationwide activity programme will share collections and widen participation, extending this mission to schools, communities and partners across the UK and online."

This will be achieved by delivering yoga, walking, dance and jogging, sessions, offering a supportive environment where participants can restore their self-esteem and mental health. These will be delivered in cohorts of 18 to 20 women for 20 weeks. column2: Over 50's Mobility & Fitness & Men Only fitness

column2: Walking Towards Unity, Health and Well-being

It combines gentle group walks, chair-based sessions and walking futsal to improve physical and mental wellbeing while building bridges between Muslim, Jewish, Christian, Sikh, Hindu, and other faith communities. Funding is for instructor costs, project co-ordination, equipment, volunteer training and promotion.

This project will provide 5 outreach sports events followed by weekly canal side water activities and multi sport for children, young people and adults who are from low income backgrounds. Funding is for coaches, management, equipment and publicity.

Rowing is not yet representative of the wider population despite strong Olympic and Paralympic success. Existing community outreach engages thousands but struggles to bridge participants into the Talent Pathway due to gaps in coaching capacity, consistency, and support. This project is aiming to address that.

This project will create two Active Recovery Spaces transforming underused areas in supported housing in Romford into an inclusive wellbeing zone for young adults aged 18-30 who have faced homelessness and trauma. this project will equip with correct flooring, compact gym tools, yoga mats, resistance bands and wellness tracking materials. Qualified coaches will activate the spaces, leading group sessions, supporting at least 30 residents with structured physical activities. Funding will cover equipment, flooring installation, coaching, admin and volunteering support costs.

This project will deliver a 24-week programme of free physical activities designed to engage inactive adults in the London Borough of Barking and Dagenham. A total of 120 open-access activity sessions will be delivered including Body Balance, Walk and Talk, Pilates with talking therapy, Aerobics for all and walking football. The project will target 100 local people per week, who are currently inactive. Funding will support coaching, staff, promotion and publicity costs.

This project will deliver weekly sessions of boxing and expand 'Power up parkies' which focus on gym sessions (cardio and strength) from one to two sessions a week for people living with Parkinson's. The Salvation Army will host a range of Christmas-themed and seasonal activities, including: a Christmas party and lunch, 88 food parcels delivered within the community, 40 Christmas gifts, 12 pampering hampers, a Christmas fun day for 30 attendees, 20 sets of toiletries, a volunteer thank you meal for 18 attendees, an outing to the Christmas Winter Illuminations at the Chelsea Royal Hospital for 30 attendees and refreshments for an outdoor community celebration.

column2: Ageing with HIV - reducing the poverty gap
column3: This project will aim to engage with and support 120 older people with HIV, by providing them with free lunches, 2 Christmas-themed dinners and take-home food parcels.

Warm Winter Connections will create a welcoming, safe space 40-50 (per session) over December to February. The project will offer weekly community gatherings that include a free hot meal, social activities, and wellbeing support for local residents, particularly older adults, young people, and families on low incomes. They will also organise 6 outings; funding would cover the cost for the mini bus hire. The project is targeted at older adults living alone, families on low incomes, and young people who are isolated or at risk of social exclusion. They aim to engage around 200 individuals over the three-month period, referred through local schools, foodbanks, GP practices, and community organisations.

Request is towards funding for K&CF Winter Warmth / Cash First initiative which supports residents who are struggling to make ends meet by paying their fuel bill or debt directly to their energy supplier, and/or providing cash support for essential items. Residents accessing either or both payments are assessed and offered specialist professional advice by one of local partner agencies, to help them improve their financial position in the longer term. This could include advice on income maximisation and accessing unclaimed benefits to which they are entitled, or on managing debt and arrears. Feedback from residents and advice agencies has indicated that this support is a lifeline for those in financial crisis, offering immediate relief, valued advice and preventing residents from taking on unmanageable debt, such as payday loans. K&CF have previously secured significant funding for this work through RBKC, but, as outlined above, this funding has now ceased due to central government cuts. Overall they will give out £240K grants to c1250 households

column3: This project will support young girls and women aged 15 to 55 from culturally diverse communities to be active. This will be achieved by running weekly yoga, exercise and fitness, and table tennis for 3 hours during a weekend. Funding will support volunteer costs, promotion, facility hire and coaching fees.

column2: Rusty Bike Shed Active Travel Project
column3: This project will support the delivery of the Rusty Bike Shed project which offers weekly guided rides for all abilities/ages, bike maintenance services, cycle confidence programs, a bike library, and affordable refurbished bikes for all abilities and ages. Funding will support a Level 3 bike mechanic for 1 day per week, cycle maintenance qualifications for staff and volunteers, and equipment hire and purchase of e-bikes, tools and consumables for bike refurbishment. The project is seeking to benefit 300 participants.

The project will deliver free courses of yoga to support the mental and physical well-being of 32 inactive adults. Four, eight-week courses of 2-hour weekly sessions will take place. The sessions will be held during weekday afternoons and will include around 30 minutes for preparation, social time and refreshments. Qualified counsellors will also be available to provide assistance and referrals into other services, if needed. Funding will pay for yoga practitioner fees, promotion, volunteer management and training, venue hire, volunteer expenses, and refreshments.

column2: More Inclusive Tandem Cycling for Visually Impaired Adults
column3: This project will support visually impaired individuals to become more active. This will be achieved by the purchase of 2 electric-assist tandems, training days for tandem pilots and 2 cycling courses for visually impaired cyclists. Funding will support the purchase of the bikes, pilot training and staffing of the courses.

This project will support the development of the Youth Activity Park, in line with Sport England's place expansion work. Funding will be used towards the construction of a multi-use space enabling activities such as skateboarding, scootering, BMX, parkour, walking and cycling.

column2: Inclusive off-road cycling at Parkwood Springs
column3: This project will purchase an additional two cycles that will allow the cycling hub at Parkwood Springs to be more accessible to people living with a disability. One of the cycles will be an electric assist handcycle for tetraplegic users, and the other will be an electric assist foot cycle for use on varied terrains. The project will conduct outreach work before delivering 50 off-road cycling sessions over the year, lasting up to 4 hours, which will be led by qualified volunteers.

column2: The Sheffield Eagles Girls' Rugby Project
column3: This project will engage girls aged 11-18 in Rugby League, addressing barriers to participation and the significant drop-off in sports in teenage girls - particularly post 16. In order to do this, the project will deliver 1.5 hours of coaching to two groups (11-14 and 15-18) outside of school and college hours. The budget will cover coaching, facility hire and equipment.

This project will deliver a multi-sport activity programme for 12 months to children, plus young people with special educational needs. Also, a two week summer camp will take place during the school holidays for 40 young people each week. Funding will support coaching costs.
The project will significantly improve the British Para Table Tennis training environment enabling athletes to adapt to new specification tables and balls for the Los Angeles Olympics cycle.

The project will deliver free, weekly coaching sessions, afterschool clubs and monthly tournaments for young and disabled people from low-income households in Cumbria, including young girls. Adapted softball and tabletop cricket activities will be introduced to support individuals with physical, sensory and learning disabilities, with the overall programme to deliver 224 sessions in 12 months, aiming to engage 200 participants and create a female development pathway at the club. Funding will support equipment, facility hire, promotion, refreshment and coaching costs, alongside costs associated with installing an accessible wheelchair ramp at the club.

This project will support the development of the Eston Recreational Ground improvements project, in line with Sport England's place expansion work. Funding will be used towards a variety of projects including the provision of a new swimming pool at the existing Eston leisure centre, and the construction of active travel routes.

column2: St Mary Bourne Community Play Space
column3: This project will resurface the MUGA (multi-use games area) situated at the Village Centre, as well as add line markings and edge the space.

This project will provide women and girls aged 13+ from the South-Asian community with opportunities to be physical active. 3-4 sessions per week will be delivered over 50 weeks using both indoor and outdoor spaces. Volunteers will also be given opportunity to gain the necessary qualifications to lead physical activity sessions beyond the project period.
This project will allow the continuation of 6 exercise classes which will be delivered weekly for one year in the local community. Funding will support facility hire and coaching costs.

column2: Sports Hall Upgrade for Bradford’s Sikh & Wider Community
column3: This project will install modern LED lighting and a ceiling ball stopping netting in the sports hall. The upgrade will improve existing provision and facilitate the introduction of new activities, including youth and ladies’ badminton coaching sessions for the Sikh and wider community in Bradford. Funding will cover facility alterations, badminton equipment and promotion costs.

column2: Climbing for All Families Continuation Project
column3: This project is a continuation of the ROKT Foundation's 'Climbing for All Families' project which has been providing accessible climbing sessions for disabled children and their families since 2022. This funding will support an additional 200 individuals over a 12 month period, expand the organisation's services by training more instructors, and introduce outdoor climbing opportunities for families. The funding will cover equipment and coach fees.

An award increase to the development of a multi-activity hub in Hillsborough Park, Sheffield that brings people together to get active. The hub will provide 3 outdoor tennis courts, a multi-sport MUGA, 2 covered paddle courts, outdoor activation space, a landscaped 9-hole mini adventure golf course, café/social space and changing rooms. The facilities will be floodlit to ensure year-round use.
