column2: "Heritage and Harmony: Preserving Panjabi Culture, Community Green Spaces and Intergenerational Bonds."
column3:
"We aim to create a thriving hub of Panjabi heritage preservation, environmental sustainability and community unity. Our vision is to safeguard Panjabi traditions by establishing a digital archive— the Sabiachar Digital Library—that will capture oral histories, cultural practices and stories for future generations. By blending these traditions with modern technology, we ensure that our rich heritage remains accessible and relevant.

In addition, we envision a community garden that promotes biodiversity and sustainable practices rooted in Panjabi agricultural knowledge. The garden will serve as a place where participants of all ages can come together, share experiences and learn about eco-friendly gardening.

Ultimately, we aim to foster intergenerational bonds, celebrate cultural diversity and create a more inclusive, vibrant community. Through workshops, festivals and cultural exchanges, we hope to build a legacy that honours the past while nurturing a sustainable, connected future for everyone involved."

"Forging a Future will build on our recent capital investment, helping us achieve future stability, economic sustainability, and aid our transition into a centre for national and international research. We would achieve a longer-term vision for our museum; opening up new funding opportunities, retain Museum Accreditation through applying for NPO and work towards securing National Status.
Funding would enable us to increase staff capacity to include a Collections Manager, Learning Manager, Events and Learning Officer, Visitor Experience and Volunteer Officer, and Tour Guides to: 
•	increase community participation 
•	to ensure equality for access and inclusion; 
•	deliver high quality learning programmes
•	retain Museum Accreditation status
•	offer guided tours to include weekends, supporting volunteer guides, enhancing visitor experience 
•	enable our senior staff to initiate partnerships and collaborative approaches 
This is to ensure we can best serve our communities, attract visitors, and enhance the museum’s economic stability."

"We want to run an intergenerational project for The Sharing Memories Group of older people and other community groups underserved by heritage in The Holme Valley, to collaboratively discover and celebrate the woollen & textile heritage of West Yorkshire.  We will teach the history of the industry to our group members, schoolchildren and other adults, bringing it to life through learning and passing on textile crafts: spinning, weaving, felting and newer techniques like yarn bombing.  We will create our own heritage scene, for a vibrant final exhibition, entitled “Woolovers”.  Central to our exhibition will be the character of Sir John Ramsden (1699-1769), an influential Huddersfield landowner who built the Cloth Hall in Huddersfield for individuals to trade cloth. Our project and exhibition will form part of Huddersfield Woven Festival 2025. We hope to achieve better community cohesion and a legacy in memories, experiences and an archived film documenting the project."

"This exciting new project will explore the rich heritage of Bangladesh with a specific focus on the impact and experiences of the Bangladeshi diaspora in the historic town of Keighley. The primary objective of our project is to preserve and share this heritage, bringing people of many different backgrounds together in celebration, unearthing new perspectives and hidden talents. The project will engage 60 people via tasters and interactive workshop sessions to explore the music, poetry and art influenced by Bangladeshi folk traditions, enabling them to develop their own works, to be showcased as part of a Keighley Bangla Mela to be held during Bradford 2025, which aims to attract 500 attendees and at least 1000 visitors to a new website."

"The Graveship of Holme - A Pageant is a heritage inclusion and access project working with hyperlocal rural communities in the Holme Valley, Kirklees, West Yorkshire to share memories, oral histories and photographs which celebrate their heritage, place, nature and landscapes.

The Graveship of Holme is an ancient administrative structure covering 7  "townships" in the valley, managed by a Constable (Grave). 

The project will remove barriers to participation for people who are under-served by heritage, making these community stories more inclusive and developing knowledge and skills within local groups. It will use visual art, drama, photography/videography to interpret the heritage to co-create public performances/events/displays shared in each township over three weekends. On the fourth weekend in June, all 7 presentations will be shared at the annual Holmfirth Arts Festival, preserving legacy through a heritage map of the Graveship, webpage, photographic exhibition and further displays at Heritage Open Days in September."

"This project will maintain and ensure the long-term survival of Portslade's Norman manor house ruins. This very rare example of a Norman manor house is Grade II* listed building and also an Ancient Scheduled Monument. The site is significant to local people as the birthplace of modern day Portslade.

We will claim back more land from the overgrown thicket areas. Here we will develop a learning space to be used for lectures, displaying of history artefacts and memorabilia, and also running our community engagement programmes and heritage outreach activities. We will develop a pop-up, sessional, Portslade museum to tour Portslade to increase engagement in local heritage.

We will run 65 free walks, talks, activities and on-line videos to retell Portslade's history, its characters and capture people's memories of its more recent past.

We will conduct further research of the conservation area, including a community archaeological dig at the manor ruins."

column2: "Saving deaf young people's culture and heritage"
column3:
"DEX is a deaf-led organisation with a deaf board, staff and deaf young members and supports the DEX Deaf Youth Council (DDYC) for deaf young people (16 to 30 years) and the DEX Deaf Youth Hub (11 to 17 years). 

This pilot project is led by the views of deaf young people and our research and literature reviews which identified there are 4,000 deaf children learning British Sign Language in the UK, thus the deaf community is consequently getting smaller. It aims to  facilitate deaf young people with creating their own deaf culture and community, to strengthen deaf identity and confidence.  

Deaf culture belongs to Deaf adults educated in deaf schools, but deaf children and young people are mostly educated in mainstream education so do not belong to either spaces. 

DEX will provide information on how human culture nurtures so  members feel loved and at home in their own community."

"This project will help St Thomas’s church take steps in preserving, understanding and sharing its unique history of inclusion. 
The project will engage the local community in recording its oral history, resulting in a creative and intergenerational celebration of local heritage, which will provide building blocks for community cohesion and identity.
The project will engage new audiences, particularly members of the LGBTQ+ community, people experiencing mental health issues, pupils from local school, and the Roman Catholic community of York, and celebrate their unique contributions to the local heritage. 
The church seeks to halt water damage to the church building, which is central to preserving the physical element of the local heritage. 
The legacy of this project will be a well thought through vision for the preservation and interpretation of the church's radical LGBTQ+ and ecumenical heritage, which may be used as the basis for future funding bids."

"Our partnership aims to address the climate and biodiversity crisis in the Doncaster-Humberhead region by accelerating nature recovery at a landscape-wide scale and connecting people to the unique environment that exists here.
We are seeking to establish the first UNESCO Biosphere Reserve in the North of England. To be successful a Biosphere must meet the needs of local people, whilst fostering a sense of ownership and pride within the community. This proposal outlines our 15-month outreach project. It’s designed to deepen our understanding of communities and raise awareness of our proposed Biosphere to inspire participation with our rich natural heritage.
Central to the outreach project are communities that traditionally have limited connections with natural heritage, due to barriers in accessing the local environment and the accompanying benefits. Undertaking a comprehensive engagement programme ensures that these underserved groups remain at the heart of our work."

column2: "Unveiling Roots: Cape Verde Heritage in the Shadows of  the Slave Trade"
column3:
"Djurtus United aims to celebrate and preserve the rich cultural heritage of the Cape Verdean community now settled in Leeds. Our project seeks to highlight Cape Verde's historical significance as a key maritime hub during the transatlantic slave trade, connecting Africa, Europe, and the Americas. By documenting oral histories, traditional
 music, dance, and customs, we will create a vibrant archive
 that reflects the community’s unique journey and contributions. 

This initiative will foster greater understanding and appreciation of Cape Verdean culture among Leeds residents, reduce social isolation, and strengthen community ties. Through educational workshops, public
 exhibitions, and community events, we will ensure that this important heritage is celebrated and preserved for future generations"

"This project is an urgent resilience application to help Wentworth Woodhouse Preservation Trust (WWPT) thrive over the coming year, implementing much needed improvements to our organisation in order to survive the short term challenges. Wentworth Woodhouse has reached a critical point in its regeneration journey. To thrive in the longer term we must develop more usable space from which to trade, in order to become financially sustainable. Lack of usable space is restricting our ability to grow as a visitor destination and business. The next capital project is a huge undertaking and will require the input of numerous funders and stakeholders. A pre-development stage is needed, to bring all the major cultural and regeneration funders to the table to agree a multi-agency approach before applications for development funding can be prepared. In the short term however, we need to survive until we move into a major development phase of works."

"Deneway's Wild Future is about expanding access to a unique green corridor running alongside a main railway line into a busy city. Deneway Nature Reserve connects wildlife to downland adjoining the city, and for local people it provides a significant door-step opportunity to engage more closely with the natural environment.  

Our project will ensure that the site is more open and accessible for the local community into the future, and to ensure that the nature reserve is in the best condition for biodiversity to flourish as a home for wildlife and a corridor for species to move through the urban landscape. 

This will also be a site for learning; providing pathways into conservation, whether this be as a volunteer (e.g. citizen scientist), a trainee ranger, ecologist or teaching practitioner.  

The project will inspire and enable local people of all ages to take lasting, practical and well-informed community-based action for nature."

"#Morethanapool will safeguard a vital community and heritage asset. Simultaneously repairing and protecting a unique building, saving stories and memories embedded in its walls, our project will put Bramley Baths on the map as an arts, culture, and heritage destination. Revitalising original spaces and facilities, and creating further opportunities for community engagement, #Morethanapool will realise untapped potential and support long term sustainability.
Symbiotic strands of increasing engagement and capital works will enable a permanent and strengthened offer around heritage, health and wellbeing, arts and culture, from a secure and sustainable building, allowing Bramley Baths to continue its 120-year-old role of serving its community.  

This project will be a vote of confidence in BB’s past, present and future: recognition of everything it has been, is now, and its potential for its next chapter, celebrating and maximising all that it is and can be for future generations.
[See Appendix 21 – Executive Summary]"

column2: "LUMB BANK – A STORIED HOUSE IN A HERITAGE LANDSCAPE"
column3:
"Arvon is a leader in literary heritage and a renowned supporter of today’s creative writers. As the owner of three historic writing houses in rural areas, we are responsible for safeguarding their future and sharing their heritage stories.  

The project at Lumb Bank in the Calder Valley, once the home of the poet Ted Hughes, will futureproof the building; produce a Conservation Management Plan for its long-term sustainability; and create a Heritage Strategy for documenting and sharing the historic Lumb Bank collection and the history of its surrounding landscape, a landscape described by Ted Hughes as ‘heavy with the dream of a people’. We will test the strategy through a consultation and events programme offering community-led heritage engagement; and we will build it into our next five-year business plan as part the Arvon North strategy to dramatically increase engagement with the landscape, literary, industrial and social heritage of the site."

column2: "Bridging Cultures: A parallel journey of teenage life in the UK and Somaliland"
column3:
"This project aims to bring together girls and young women from diverse backgrounds to work on a project looking at their Somali heritage.  They will undertake research and a creative project that will include researching and recording Somali women's heritage, traditions and culture, and then using this to write, produce and perform a play.
The play will explore parallel experiences of growing up as a teenager in the UK and in Somaliland, offering insights into cultures, values and challenges.

Through interviewing their mothers and older women within the community, the girls will gain a deeper perspective on the lives of previous generations.   

They will craft costumes, create a set, learn traditional dance, and build a creative narrative that bridges the gap between these two worlds, fostering understanding, dialogue and cultural pride."

column2: "Children’s Capital of Culture – You’re Not from New York City, You’re from Rov’Rum"
column3:
"In 2025 Rotherham becomes the world’s first Children’s Capital of Culture. Responding to this pivotal moment in our history, 25 community-based Heritage Producers aged 16-25 will:
• develop the skills, confidence and networks to enable the preservation of Rotherham’s past and future heritage, through forging new connections and developing communities’ sense of identity, belonging and pride of place 
• utilise their generation’s ‘born-digital’ skills to build an “Archive of Memories”, focusing on contemporary collecting and digital preservation to modernise approaches to archival engagement
• work alongside Rotherham Archives to capture and preserve our shared history as it unfolds, and reach across the generations to connect this with our borough’s traditional community and social heritage
• collaborate with a renowned Guest Director to deliver a major new creative commission that draws inspiration from the “Archive of Memories” to interrogate who we are, where we come from and where might go next"

"Set within the atmospheric Ironbridge Gorge in Shropshire, are a collection of museums, historic sites and structures owned and operated by the Ironbridge Gorge Museum Trust (IGMT).  The birthplace of the Industrial Revolution, this World Heritage Site is an internationally significant and locally loved place that celebrates industrial heritage.  

Increasing financial pressures means that the National Trust (NT) are in discussions about acquiring IGMT’s assets and taking over the operational management of their sites.  This would safeguard IGMT’s built heritage and stories of the Industrial Revolution for future generations to enjoy. 

The NT now needs to complete a feasibility study and due diligence around the asset transfer to prepare a comprehensive business case and operating model.  We are seeking support from the Heritage Fund towards this process, which will run from April to September 2025."
column14: The National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty

column3:
"The WWII armoured wagon, a key wartime artifact of the Romney, Hythe & Dymchurch Railway (RH&DR), is being restored for the RH&DR Centenary in 2027. Previously reconstructed in the 1990s using a plywood replica, it deteriorated, leading to a renewed effort to create a durable replica using modern materials.

Early work included CAD drawings and shot-blasting, but the project stalled due to frame corrosion and COVID-19. Recent progress with detailed specifications and costings has brought it back on track, with restoration costs estimated at £28,176.83.

The project will preserve wartime history, enhance visitor experiences with reenactments and exhibits, and engage the community through educational workshops. It links RH&DR’s heritage to broader WWII and local climate change narratives, creating a lasting educational and cultural legacy.

Support will ensure this unique artifact continues to inspire and educate future generations."
column14: Romney, Hythe and Dymchurch Railway Supporters Association

column2: "Swallowed By The Waves: lost wonders of Brighton seafront"
column3:
"We wish to achieve greater public understanding and enjoyment of Brighton’s seafront  leisure heritage and make it more accessible to parts of our local community currently facing barriers. We believe this will allow our organisation to achieve greater resilience as a seafront stakeholder.  

We will do this by marking the 50th anniversary of the closure to the public of Brighton West Pier with a multi-media display and roadshow on the seafront to celebrate the legacy not only of the pier itself but also of its bygone neighbouring marvels: The Royal Suspension Chain Pier; the Victorian ‘Daddy Long Legs’ boat-on-a-train-track; and the ‘Brighton Queen’ paddle steamers. 

We will be able to achieve our goals by delivering the project not just to seafront visitors and local schools but also to dementia sufferers, single male parents at risk of isolation, and to low-income families with access barriers to enrichment activities."

"Our project will ensure the Foundation for Common Land (FCL) can support a brighter future for the outstanding natural, cultural and archaeological heritage of England’s 400,000 ha of Common Land – visited by >30 million/yr. 
As the only national charity working to improve this much-loved yet threatened heritage, we will do this by building our organisation’s resilience.
Our delivery is rapidly expanding, and we’ve experienced a steep learning curve leading to an unprecedented demand for our services. 
We must change, and develop our capacity for a national-scale action network. We will: 
-	Develop an ambitious organisational strategy – creating a fit-for-purpose charity that is resilient and well-governed
-	Formulate plans for financial sustainability to deliver at the scale heritage and people need 
-	Trial new audience engagement with Common Land’s heritage. 
The project is a springboard to socially, financially and environmentally sustainable Common Land, and Commons communities"

"The Sensational Alzana’s and Other Daredevils! project, will celebrate and preserve Maltby’s unique cultural heritage by bringing the extraordinary story of Harold Alzana and his family to life. By blending historical preservation, creative workshops, and exciting live performances, the project will connect people across generations to their shared history.

We envision a vibrant and inclusive programme that engages 1,500+ participants directly, using circus arts to inspire creativity and community spirit. By collecting and archiving oral histories, the project ensures the Alzana’s legacy is safeguarded for future generations while sparking a borough-wide conversation about the importance of local heritage and stories.

The project is a celebration of the past and a catalyst for new artistic and cultural exploration, leaving a lasting legacy of engagement, pride, and connection for Maltby and beyond."

"Common Threads will be a year-round programme of weaving activities culminating each September in a festival in central Sheffield celebrating and showcasing textile crafts from around the world. 

This project grew from a collaboration between arts company The Bare Project and the Higsad Alool Weavers, who practice heritage weaving from the nomadic Somali diaspora. We expanded this collaboration to include 3 other women’s weaving groups to co-produce workshops sharing textile practices. Together we hosted our first pilot of Common Threads festival in 2024. 

This work demonstrated a significant need for this project—to protect heritage crafts, celebrate cross-cultural exchange, and promote sustainable relationships with textiles. In recognition of this need, we want to scale-up Common Threads into a long-term programme - to support community weaving, to raise the profile of these disappearing heritage craft practices and to celebrate the rich and diverse textile crafts practiced in Sheffield today."

"Roots in the River will connect people to the natural and industrial heritages on the River Worth, Fagley Beck and other smaller becks in the Bradford area, with the aim of creating sustainable volunteering efforts designed to improve the rivers.
We will do this through walks, talks and practical volunteering events designed to highlight the importance of those connections and of restoring the rivers and becks. 
Where possible we will focus on communities, such as BME and socially/economically disadvantaged,  traditionally under-represented in the environment and who typically spend less time and effort visiting and renovating our rivers."

"Forewarned is Forearmed will activate the 100th anniversary of the Royal Observer Corps (ROC), a nationwide defence network who monitored Britain’s skies. Centred on the last preserved Cold War Bunker, located in York, English Heritage (EH) and delivery partner Digital Drama will capture oral histories from ROC volunteers, preserving their testimony before it is lost. A press release and launch event will share a new recording of the WINTEX-CIMEX nuclear threat training script, intriguing the public. Local people will be trained to use archives and co-create digital outputs, progressing to form the bunker’s first cohort of volunteers. An interactive ‘Discovery’ tour will extend the bunker’s school offer to younger pupils and a new public tour will be inspired by oral histories. Milestone events a panel at the York Festival of Ideas and an immersive centenary celebration. Accessible digital records will create a legacy, keeping the ROC’s heritage in public consciousness."

"MD North supports museums across the north of England and is managed by a partnership between York Museums Trust, Manchester Museums Partnership, Cumbria Museum Consortium and North East Museums.

MD North will deliver a Future Preparedness programme enabling museums in the North of England to: 
-Respond to and prepare for current and future climate disruptions through training, grants and support 
-Take a data driven approach to understand and manage environmental risks 
-Take a holistic approach to sustainable management to better protect buildings, estates and collections now and for the future 
-Pursue mitigation, adaptation and resilience to inform climate action strategies for future sustainability 
-Develop effective emergency plans, responding to current and future risks 
-Develop skills in collections salvage following environmental incidents? 
-Access funding, advice and peer support opportunities to progress plans for long-term resilience  
-Secure and collate data and information needed for advocacy and to secure capital funding"

column2: "IOU at 50 - Building the North’s Hidden Super City"
column3:
"IOU, a pioneering force in experimental, site-specific art, aims to conserve its 50-year legacy by capturing and bringing to life rare props, images, unseen films, and personal accounts from artists, sector leaders, audiences, and communities across the UK influenced by its work. The project will place IOU’s legacy within the broader historical context of social and technological change in Calderdale and beyond.

This work is integral to our Creation Centre vision, providing communities with opportunities to engage with arts heritage, develop skills and creativity. As part of this, our long-term home at Dean Clough Mills requires enhanced archive facilities, including improved storage and digitisation solutions, ensuring accessibility.

Approaching our 50th anniversary in 2026, we will continue bridging art, engineering, technology, and the natural environment through heritage initiatives that inspire artistic and community responses. This investment will expand access to both physical and non-physical heritage, ensuring its relevance for future generations."

"We’ll preserve the Oral Histories of 150 working-class people from five former industrial communities in Wakefield District.

We’ll build on a successful pilot which digitally preserved 30 untold stories from Castleford’s coal-mining community. These Oral Histories were exhibited at National Trust’s Nostell Priory, reaching a wide audience, and encouraging working-class-visitors. They’re being preserved digitally for posterity/permanent access by Wakefield Museums, filling an identified gap. 

The five new areas have equally strong industrial heritage, including glass-making, boat-building, textiles and coal-mining where most local people derived their livelihoods. These industries have now all but gone. As workers/family members pass-away, their stories will be lost forever unless we act now. 

Working with local groups/historical societies, we’ll capture 30 Oral Histories of working-class life per community around specific themes. Wakefield Museums/Libraries will run local exhibitions and preserve the recordings digitally. Six major Wakefield heritage sites/shopping centres will exhibit the Oral Histories, attracting working-class visitors."

column2: "BluePRINT: Creating a regional centre of printmaking"
column3:
""BluePRINT" would support WYPW's organisational sustainability and plan for the creation of a new heritage arts centre: West Yorkshire Print Workshop's Northern Centre for Print. This project would engage, and consult with, stakeholders to plan and co-design a centre to widen participation in the heritage of, and contemporary use, of print. This would be through:
1.) Research and drawing together the heritage story of printmaking in West Yorkshire to inform future programming
2.) Create a space needs appraisal for WYPW's future to ensure heritage skills are passed on in a centre of excellence
3.) To assess the business modelling, centring around traditional and heritage printmaking and a place to grow creative jobs, and carry out market research to inform this
4.) Commissioning work to identify building options (in heritage buildings) and carry out condition surveys and initial costings and drawings for these buildings; in preparation for future funding bids."

column2: "Developing Standardised Biodiversity Metrics and Financial Tools for Peatlands and Woodlands"
column3: "Our goal with this project is to further develop a viable biodiversity methodology for Peatland and Woodland in Scotland. The Woodland Carbon Code (WCC) and Peatland Code (PC) have set high integrity standards and have made significant progress in understanding the emerging biodiversity market. There is a strong interest in quantifying biodiversity and the metrics which have been developed for these habitats are viable. The FIRNS 1 project produced a methodology for baselining biodiversity quantification. Feedback from public and academic sources highlighted missing datasets crucial for successful implementation. This next phase focuses on data aggregation and analysis to estimate credit potential for sites, create a community similarity index to contextualise results for UK woodlands and peatlands, and refine the framework for better accessibility and uptake."
column14: The Royal Society of Wildlife Trusts

column3:
"This project will enable the Featherstone Rovers Foundation to properly care for its collection, train staff in storytelling, gather significant objects, and acquire the necessary equipment to preserve and display its heritage. It will strengthen the Foundation’s relationship with the National Coal Mining Museum of England (NCMME), while bringing to light the rich oral history and historical memorabilia that showcase the mining industry's connection to rugby league. The project will highlight the role of women in rugby league and engage both the community and new audiences with this heritage, ensuring it is not lost over time.

The project's legacy will expand the heritage story throughout the district, reaching rugby fans who are not typically part of traditional heritage audiences. It will include an inspiring digital exhibition, improved collections management and display, the creation of new networks, including with NCMME, and the fostering of a stronger community spirit."

column2: "Defining a Decade: A 10-year masterplan for Sheffield Museums"
column3:
"Defining a Decade will refine and focus Sheffield Museums’ ambition to become a progressive, resilient and sustainable organisation. Rooted in Sheffield, the museums will enrich life in the city, connecting people with their heritage and creating welcoming and inspiring museum experiences for everyone. 

Outputs include;
•	a holistic organisational and estate masterplan
•	agile and realistic delivery plans 
•	a 5-year business plan.

We will prioritise activity across capital project planning, income generation, creative programming, collections development, measuring impact and identifying and mitigating risk. This project will invest in our teams’ skills and capacity and nurture an adaptive, collaborative organisation that makes a sustainable contribution to Sheffield and the communities we serve. 

Defining a Decade will develop a clear strategy to guide us through this globally challenging period to a fruitful future, safeguarding previous NLHF investment and actively contributing to a vibrant Sheffield that understands and values its rich heritage."

column2: "The Hepworth Wakefield / Wakefield Art Collection New Acquisition: Barbara Hepworth, Sculpture with Colour (Oval Form) Pale Blue and Red, 1943"
column3:
"The Hepworth Wakefield (THW) wishes to acquire an exceptional artwork by Barbara Hepworth, currently under export deferral granted by the Secretary of State, owing to its importance in the development of Modernism in Britain and its connection to national life during World War II. We have five months to raise £3.78m to save this important sculpture for the nation. 

If successful in our fundraising, we will ensure the sculpture, which has been in private ownership since its creation in 1943, goes on public display in the city of Hepworth’s birth (Wakefield) where everyone can experience the work first-hand. Here it will be shown alongside the numerous contemporary artists Hepworth has inspired, as well as in the context of our significant collection of Modern British art. This project will give our local audiences and stakeholders pride and continued confidence in our work and help raise our profile nationally and internationally."
column11: National Lottery Heritage Grants £250,000 to £10 million

column3:
"We aim to find a permanent home for Hampshire's Strawberry Story, celebrating the region's rich agricultural heritage and the significance of the strawberry industry. By creating an engaging and informative display, we plan to share the historical and cultural impact of strawberry farming in Hampshire. Central to this project is the conservation of the historic strawberry wagon, a unique object that symbolises the county's agricultural past.  

The legacy of our project will be the creation of a co-produced display that highlights the significant impact of the strawberry industry on Hampshire. Our project will tell a broader narrative, including the stories of local workers, market trends, and the community's connection to the strawberry industry. This includes the conservation of the strawberry wagon, ensuring this object is conserved and in better condition. Our efforts will also enhance community engagement and deepen the understanding of the county's cultural heritage."

column2: "#NTC Bradford’s Green Blue Steppingstones – Connecting People and Nature Across Our Towns and City"
column3:
"Bradford’s Green Blue Steppingstones envisions revitalising public green and blue spaces to enhance health, community engagement, and biodiversity. By mapping habitat networks, it aims to improve ecological connectivity while fostering community well-being. Collaborating with local partners through co-design ensures inclusivity and resilience, while engaging land asset owners unlocks the potential of green infrastructure. A targeted communication strategy will raise public awareness, share success stories, and inspire community involvement, empowering partners and promoting innovative ideas.
The project seeks sustainable models for maintaining blue-green infrastructure, balancing affordability, and biodiversity. By facilitating knowledge sharing and fostering partnerships, it aims to strategies needed for a thriving network of urban parks and green spaces. This initiative also prioritises educational resources to inspire younger generations, promoting environmental stewardship. Overall, the project aspires to transform urban spaces into vibrant hubs of health, local pride, and ecological harmony, benefiting communities for generations to come."
column14: City of Bradford Metropolitan District Council

column2: "#NTC Tees Urban Nature Network: Connecting communities and restoring natural heritage"
column3:
"Our vision is for an urban Teesside rich in natural heritage, with local communities empowered to reclaim, restore and reimagine their green and blue spaces, fostering vibrant hubs for connection, recreation and environmental stewardship. Using a place-based whole system approach, we will create the conditions for change to ensure urban green/blue spaces thrive, are safer, accessible and reflective of the unique character and needs of our communities. We will collaborate to put the value of green/blue spaces at the heart of decision making, so that communities and organisations can take pride in, and care for, their natural assets.
Our programme will capitalise on our unique natural and people assets, to tackle the complex challenge of creating a unified response across diverse partners and communities, recognising that we will need courage to radically change how the development and management of green/blue spaces will be tackled now and in the future."

column2: "Bussing Out: Recovering the Forgotten Histories of Britain's Post-War Migrant Generations"
column3:
"Bussing Out is an immersive installation illuminating a vital neglected aspect of Britain's post-war heritage — the policy of ‘bussing’ Black and Asian children from inner cities to rural schools from the 60s to 80s, ensuring no school had “over 30 immigrants on roll”.

A national tour of an expanded installation will go to six locations including cities where bussing happened. Through wrap-around activity we will expand the oral history archive of those who were bussed, recovering and safeguarding a critically under-represented chapter of social history. We will ensure memories, testimonies, and experiences of those affected are documented and preserved.

We will embed this history within Britain’s wider diverse heritage narrative, creating a legacy through a publicly accessible digital archive and educational resources benefitting schools, researchers, and communities. We will centre the voices of this lived history, challenging omissions within our national memory and inspire more inclusive approaches to heritage."

column2: "Beyond the Try Line –  Celebrating Community Heritage in Rugby"
column3:
"In 2025, the British Asian Rugby Association C.I.C (BARA) celebrates 20 years of promoting equality and inclusion in rugby. Established in Bradford in 2004, with backing from local councils and national sporting bodies, BARA has worked to break cultural and religious barriers, increasing South Asian participation in rugby league and union.
This project honours the pioneers—men and women—who challenged the norms of a predominantly white sport. By sharing their stories, we aim to highlight their contributions to rugby and the wider push for diversity and representation.
Aligned with Bradford’s status as UK City of Culture 2025, the project will showcase BARA’s legacy through events and educational initiatives across West Yorkshire.
By documenting this history, we not only celebrate past achievements but also inspire future generations to continue building an inclusive future for rugby and sport in general. It’s a tribute to resilience, representation, and lasting change."

column2: "Diversifying Engagement with Brass Band Heritage: Sharing the Story with Young People"
column3: "This project is focused on sharing the brass band story and engaging young people with brass band heritage and the wider social and family histories contained within the popular and growing collection of the Brass Bands Archive (BBA). Throughout this project we will collect oral histories with a particular focus on communities who are under-represented, preserve brass band ephemera that would have been lost otherwise, create opportunities for children to engage with local heritage, and help young people develop skills through paid internships, underpinning the future of this important national collection and inspiring a new and more diverse generation of brass band players and audiences. 2028 will see the 60th anniversary of Brass Bands England (BBE), presenting an exciting opportunity to improve access to this internationally significant archive and put in place activities to drive the sector forward over the following decades."

column2: "Mojo Rising - Celebrating 60 Years Of Music And Community"
column3: "Our vision for the project is to celebrate and conserve the remarkable legacy of a venue that was at the heart of Sheffield's pop culture revolution during the mid-1960s. We aim to illustrate its significant influence on music, fashion, and youth culture and the fact it was based in the seemingly unlikely area of suburban Pitsmoor . Through engaging exhibitions, interactive workshops a comprehensive digital archive and more, we aspire to educate and inspire both current and future generations about the transformative power of King Mojo and the artists that performed. By reconnecting the Pitsmoor community with this vibrant part of their heritage on the club's anniversary, we hope to foster a deeper appreciation and pride in the musical and social history of one of the city's most deprived areas, ensuring that the spirit of King Mojo continues to enrich lives across generations."

column2: "Brathay Blueprint - Buildings, Boats and Brighter Futures"
column3:
"We will use Brathay’s 80-year heritage to build brighter futures. This project will help conserve our historic estate, boat fleet, and archive, making them more accessible and relevant. We’ll protect craft skills, connect people to nature, and celebrate outdoor learning—empowering young people and underrepresented groups, and ensuring Brathay’s legacy continues to inspire, include, and transform lives. The project will:
Create a Blueprint to identify best long-term sustainable use and sensitive adaptation of our historic estate and heritage buildings for future users.
Identify a route-map for future investment and sustainable development opportunities at Brathay.
Uncover, record and present hidden stories of Brathay's pioneering past.
Professionally curate and make accessible the Brathay Archive of the Outdoor Learning Movement.
Whilst conserving our heritage boat fleet, we’ll activate our Heritage Boat Conservation Skills succession plan.
Celebrate our heritage and launch our future at our special 80th year events in 2026."

"The project will educate the school children of Barnsley in the rich sporting heritage of the mines and miners that once populated the town. Many young people will use a former miners welfare for recreational sport we want them to know why it is there and what sports and past time the miners would have enjoyed. We want the former miners to be the ones going into schools and telling their stories first hand. They will complete talks and then run sports sessions for the children with the assistance of our sports staff. The miners will also complete recorded sessions so these memories are not lost. we will use each surviving miners welfare as a base to then run sports and games days for local schools. On each welfare we would like an interactive board with a QR code which will take user to the oral histories collected online."

"We will protect our future and celebrate our past, in the run-up to our bicentennial celebrations.  We will explore key aspects of our community’s heritage and history, and involve a wide range of people in doing so, and in parallel we will make changes to our building that take us towards net zero.

Our net zero interventions will help us to continue to provide low-cost facilities for the hundreds or people who use our historic building every week.  

We see the heritage of the church and town, and its environmental future, as being closely linked.  Our church founders are buried within the church, a tribute to the social action inspired by Methodism.  In this 80th anniversary of VE Day, we have extensive records of Wetherby war dead, and the sacrifice they made.  Now, we want to secure our legacy and environment for future generations."

column2: "The History of Castleford and District Amateur Rugby League"
column3: "We will tell the story of Amateur Rugby League in the Castleford area, from it’s inception in the late 1890’s to present day. Working with community clubs we will identify key volunteers, many are active on a local facebook group, to help us collect, collate, record the history of amateur clubs enabling us to build innovative mini museums featuring each club, past and present, with information about their club. We will host training workshops at local clubs to upskill volunteers to develop skills in digitisation, research, presentation methods, interview skills to record oral histories of older players, officials and volunteers to capture their memories. Our project will reconnect past players and supporters with their club, create a network of club “historians” who will add to our story for years to come further embedding their club in our community brining new and old together to enhance the club environment for all."

column2: "Cripping Culture: a Journey into Disability Arts Heritage"
column3:
"’Cripping Culture: a Journey into Disability Arts Heritage’ will research and reveal the achievements of the disabled artists and activists who put disability rights on the map from the late 1970s onwards. (Cripping, like queering, uses a reclaimed word to apply a disability lens to culture). Through mass community participation we will capture memories about elders and changemakers who established disability arts as a cornerstone of socially engaged practice and transformed the UK’s arts and culture landscape. 

From interviews, research, and work to publish our own archive, an interactive digital timeline will provide extensive interpretation for people to engage with the heritage. This will safeguard the heritage of the Disability Arts movement, fill gaps in existing knowledge, enable generations of disabled people to connect with their heritage, and increase public understanding of the journeys of artists and activists who have campaigned for the human rights of disabled people."

"Cookham Abbey is the 'lost' Anglo-Saxon royal monastery forgotten for 1,200 years, ruled by Mercian Queen Cynethryth and set in the sacred landscape of the Middle Thames.  'Cookham Abbey Connects' is a new year-round engagement project responding to local and national interest in the dig. Partners University of Reading (UoR) and Friends of Cookham Abbey (FCA) will increase heritage interpretation and conservation, co-create new learning opportunities and link communities representing the vibrant mix of cultures and faiths locally to the spiritual sites of the middle Thames region. Cookham Abbey's rich archaeology will be the catalyst for engagement. With three month-long annual digs confirmed, we will capitalise on the momentum of each dig to enable hundreds more people from diverse backgrounds to participate year-round, sharing the region's fascinating heritage in exciting, relevant and accessible ways. We'll embed understanding about this sacred landscape across our communities and build a sustainable, UK-wide legacy."

column2: "#LC HEART. Heritage, Environment and Resilience Together"
column3: "The Lake District World Heritage Site faces growing threats from climate change - flooding, biodiversity loss and rising temperatures are already putting its landscapes, traditions and global significance at risk. This project will deliver fast, practical action to tackle those risks head-on, whilst building a long-term strategy for climate resilience rooted in heritage and community. Led by LDF and delivered in partnership with LDNPA and established stakeholder networks, the project will combine research, engagement and on-the-ground delivery. Communities, landowners and existing groups will shape the response-informing a climate and action plan, contributing to the WHS interpretation plan and driving ten community-led pilot projects which focus on climate resilience and WHS interpretation. This is not just a response to climate change, it is a bold, place-based commitment to protect the Lake District’s Outstanding Universal Value, now and for the future. A powerful first step in a larger, landscape-scale connection."

column2: "REVERB. Echoes of Barrow in Furness Music Scenes."
column3:
"REVERB will preserve and celebrate the heritage of Barrow-in Furness' grass-roots pop music industry over several decades. In partnership with our local museum, archives and practitioners, we will produce a community Pop Culture Archive for Barrow, accessible physically and online. Public calls and research will provide ephemera and anecdotes from musicians, audience members,  promoters, record shop owners and designers through coffee mornings, oral history sessions, research events and workshops, at our base in Barrow Park and other public realm spaces.
REVERB will collect voices, memories and artefacts from within a cultural industry of creativity and entrepreneurialism that grew from our community in response to its enthusiasms. REVERB creates a point of intersection between personal memory and civic history. It will be valued by local people who provide the material, by the inheritors of the scenes they created, and by new generations looking for positive and engaging histories of their town."

"In an area of low engagement we, the local people
will bring our Viking heritage back to life. Our goal is increasing the diversity of people engaging with heritage by forming new community partnerships and using innovative methods.
Young people, volunteers, refugees, heritage enthusiast groups and
asylum seekers are signed up!
The Vikings were here over a thousand
years ago and seem distant and mysterious. We will make them real again through exciting performances, art,
games and even a viking feast! 
The Furness Viking hoard is the biggest ever to have been found in our
area, and has been described as a "missing link" as it is
the first significant archaeological evidence of Norse
inhabitation in Furness. The places we live (Barrow,
Yarlside, Roa Island and Ormsgill) were named by Norse
men and women. We need to find out more! 
Come and join us!"

column2: "60 Years of Music – the story of Leeds Conservatoire"
column3:
"We wish to celebrate and preserve the first 60 years of Leeds Conservatoire’s impact on the city it serves. We will do this using three areas of activity: forming an archive of newly discovered material previously assumed lost; creation of new archival material and data such as oral histories and metadata; creative, bespoke, audience-focused heritage activities inspired by our pioneering first six decades.  

We are excited to collaborate with Leeds City Museum on a six-month exhibition. Working with music communities and cultural organisations, the exhibition will weave our stories into the city’s musical history. This exhibition and events programme will bring these stories together for the first time, igniting ways to maintain these new avenues via which residents, visitors and students will feel a part of the city’s cultural prowess. This supports the conservatoire’s long-term aim: to be a touchstone for celebrating Leeds intersectional musical past and present."

"Rotherham United Community Trust, the charitable arm of Rotherham United Football Club, is dedicated to uniting and empowering our communities. Guided by our vision, Everyone in Rotherham: United, successful, and living well, this project supports social cohesion, heritage, and inclusion through the power of football.

To mark RUFC’s 100th anniversary, we will explore the club’s rich history through the voices of fans, players, and local communities. Personal memories, creative arts, and digital storytelling will chart RUFC’s journey from its founding in 1925 to the present day at the New York Stadium, creating a lasting legacy for future generations.

In response to the divisions felt after last summer’s riots, we will use football to bring people together and celebrate diversity. Our work will highlight progress in equality, including the rise of women’s football, improved access for disabled players, and increased representation from the global majority in the game."

column2: "The Big K – The Pit That Shaped a Community"
column3: "The Big K – The Pit That Shaped a Community, is a creative heritage film project developed in partnership with former coal miners and families from Kellingley Colliery, the UK’s last deep coal mine. Marking a decade since its closure, the film captures the voices of those who lived through this pivotal moment, some now volunteers and guides at the National Coal Mining Museum, others based across Wakefield. It reflects on the mine’s legacy and its enduring impact on the community. By sharing short clips on social media, the project aims to engage younger audiences, helping them explore how coal, community, and resilience shaped Wakefield’s identity. Aligned with Wakefield’s Heritage Framework: Our Heritage, Our Stories, the project uplifts working-class narratives, promotes community storytelling, uses heritage to foster identity, inclusion, and belonging. Public screenings invite viewers to reflect, respond, and share their own memories, deepening connections to the region’s mining heritage."

column2: "The Gresley 150 Experience: Celebrating Engineering & Innovation in Doncaster"
column3:
"The project will commemorate the 150th anniversary of the birth of Sir Nigel Gresley on 19 June 26 who lived and worked in Doncaster. We will achieve this through:

•	A permanent small exhibition at the Danum Gallery, Library & Museum in Doncaster, augmented by a temporary larger display in 2026.
•	Interpretation of his life story and its relevance including his works and legacy through records and artefacts of the Gresley Society and project partners.
•	The development of our interpretation and learning offer to support outreach and to engage with new and particularly younger audiences. 
•	Creation of a film to explain his life, works and significance.
•	Safe storage & public access to The Gresley Society and partner organisations’ disbursed archives, artefacts and libraries.
•	Digitisation of key records of The Gresley Society and other partner organisations
•	A symposium to be held in 2026."

"September 2025 marks the 40th anniversary of the founding of Northern School of Contemporary Dance. We will seize this opportunity to spark a year of community activity, uncovering, exploring and celebrating the extraordinary mix of cultures, influences and people in Chapeltown/Harehills that seeded our school into being, and that remain embodied in its ethos and creative expression. We want to capture this heritage through the living memories of the many, diverse communities whose story this is: the young West Indian generation of the 70s/80s, whose talents transformed the world of dance; their mothers and families; the visionary teachers whose ambition for their pupils knew no limits; the Jewish community whose beautiful Grade II listed ‘New Synagogue’ is now home to our Riley Theatre. They will create a kaleidoscope of stories and perspectives, that will be shared and celebrated through community performances/events and captured for future generations in NSCD’s own archives."

"Our project, Unheard Leeds, preserves and shares the rich but often overlooked social heritage of three marginalized groups in Leeds: older LGBTQ+ people, people seeking asylum, and women who are unpaid carers and parents. This is an oral histories project that captures lived experiences and stories that reflect wider historical change over the past 50–75 years in Leeds, including shifts in migration, gender roles, LGBTQ+ rights, and community cohesion.

By recording personal testimonies and connecting them with local historical events and movements, we will create a living archive of local social history. Through creative methods, formal archiving and public performances, we will make this heritage accessible to the wider community, ensuring these important narratives are valued, preserved, and celebrated."

"MUTTON is a project, including: 

-MUTTON: a piece of theatre telling the story of Mary Bateman, exploring parallels between poverty in the 1800s and today.
-Young Company: creative research and performance project co-led by young people (YP) at risk of becoming NEET, exploring untold stories of individuals from communities they belong to.
-Community Storytelling: workshops and events for adults, sharing local heritage through storytelling.

MUTTON will contribute to more inclusive, representative understanding of Leeds’ heritage - centred on the complexity, creativity, and resilience of communities often left out of traditional histories. The project will empower YP to explore cultural and social histories through creative research and performance. Developing skills in communication, research, and performance; building confidence and a deeper connection to heritage.

The MUTTON legacy: 
1 x play toured to disadvantaged communities
3 x youth-led performances
2 x storytelling performances by adults
A creative online archive of untold stories"

"The aim of our Project is two-fold:
•         to achieve completion of our internal phased refurbishment programme
•         to implement a programme of Know Your City activities and events which celebrate Bradford’s diverse heritage and make us more widely known  
Capital aspects will focus on accessibility issues identified in a recent Audit of our historic building and will comprise the reconfiguration and upgrade of WC facilities adjacent to the second-floor meeting rooms, the widening of doorways and refurbishment of the stair core to improve accessibility and enhance visitor experience on all levels of the building.
The Events are designed to answer the many questions we are asked about why we were founded 200 years ago, who we served, what we do today and what we can do in the future?"

"Building on the success of NLHF “Bats in Churches”, Natural England, Church of England, Churches Conservation Trust, Bat Conservation Trust, and Caring for God’s Acre are pooling expertise for a four-year England-wide project that:
Broadens engagement: reaching 130K people, prioritising underserved communities, to enable enjoyment of natural/cultural heritage through NightWatch events, school sessions, Challenge Badges, hands-on workshops and online connections.
Supports practical action: working across c. 75ha priority habitat (2,400ha+ indirectly) benefiting 23+ protected species. We’ll work with 150 Sacred Places to develop management plans that deliver for built and natural heritage, and people. We’ll involve more volunteers to deliver better access, enhance biodiversity, and enable care of built heritage with specialist cleaning workshops/small equipment.
Builds professional capacity: provide tailored training for 740+ individuals including CPD opportunities. We’ll create apprenticeship/undergraduate training opportunities to inspire new generation of ecologists/building specialists. We’ll share specialist information via online training and professionals’ forums."

column2: "A new future for the iconic Middle Street Synagogue"
column3:
"Our vision is to secure a sustainable future for Middle Street Synagogue by detailing plans for its transformation into a Jewish Cultural Centre offering a dynamic cultural, educational and heritage offer for the local community and visitors. 

The project responds to urgent risks identified in a recent condition survey as well as to the pressing need to find a wider sustainable use for the building - closed for over two decades. Without action, the physical fabric, historic and public value of this exceptional Grade II* listed site is at risk.

We will undertake stabilisation works, commission specialist surveys to inform future works, and develop interim governance to support longer-term delivery and operations. The legacy will be a costed, inclusive and credible plan for restoration and reuse, backed by consultation, new partnerships and a fundraising development plan, ready to secure investment and bring this unique heritage site back into civic life."

column2: "Connecting Neighbourhoods, Nature and Heritage: Whitehawk’s Hills"
column3:
"Our vision is for Whitehawk’s Hills to become a vibrant, inclusive heritage and nature site, cared for and celebrated by its local community.   

Whitehawk Hill & Encampment is one of Britain’s earliest Neolithic monuments, a place where communities came together to share stories and make bonds. Its cultural and natural heritage are deeply connected - with Neolithic farming creating the chalk grassland which supports one of Britain’s richest biodiversity. The encampment is 1,000 years older than Stonehenge, yet under-visited, under-celebrated and poorly understood.

Placing local people at the heart of design and delivery, this project will reconnect East Brighton residents with their heritage through inclusive guided walks, new trails, heritage crafts, community activities, AR interpretation and volunteering. 

Together, the Trust for Developing Communities and six grassroots community organisations, will leave a legacy of pride, participation and sustainable, community-led stewardship of this unique Scheduled Monument and Local Nature Reserve."

column2: "Bevin Boys: forgotten stories of WW2 in Sheffield"
column3:
"Bevin Court support people who are homeless, have learning disabilities, mental health problems or substance/alcohol use problems. 
Aims:
•To explore the mining heritage of the site as a training camp used for the Bevin Boys during WW2 and what remains. 
•Work with the community in the area to protect our wildlife habitats around the grounds. 
•To maintain the Local Wildlife Site, Local Green Space/Ancient Woodland designations of the adjacent valley. 
•Interpret the site for the community, staff, residents so that it is valued and cherished, not only for its heritage but as a wild space. 
•Provide a place for outdoor education, for birdwatching and is a place to learn about flora and fauna. 
•Improve the habitats of the orchard
•Provide a place to walk, to run, to spend time alone, or with family and friends, providing physical and mental health benefits, offering peace and tranquility for the wider community."

column2: "Daphne Oram at 100: Pioneer of Electronic Sound and Music"
column3:
"This project celebrates the birth centenary of Daphne Oram, – pioneering electronic composer and founder of the BBC’s Radiophonic Workshop - whose huge body of work (composition, techniques, inventions) remains little known despite being a vital force in the development of electronic music. Oram’s influence as a role model for women is not to be underestimated.

As the result of a widely circulated consultation survey gathering 60+ responses, and 5 interviews, we know that awareness of her work is extremely mixed - some (largely academics) being enthusiastic experts, whereas others struggle to pinpoint the name.

This heritage project exists to bring Oram’s work to a larger, more diverse audience, at a time where the playing field for women and gender minority composers and music tech professionals remains distinctly unbalanced. In our consultation, the current environment was described as “intimidating”, “male-dominated” with gender-based discrimination an “almost everyday” occurrence."

column2: "Lakeland Arts: Connecting Kendal's Heritage, Community, and Ecology"
column3:
"We will develop the strategic foundations for a resilient, inclusive, and future-focused heritage offer at the Lakeland Museum and Abbot Hall site, Kendal. Through a structured process of planning, consultation, and evaluation, we will create a comprehensive plan that ensures the long-term impact and care of our heritage assets.
The project will centre on three interlinked workstreams: Digital & Technology – creating a new strategy that streamlines operations and creates opportunities for engagement; Capital – creating a Master Plan, Feasibility Study and Options Appraisal for the site, collections and existing buildings. Environmental Sustainability – developing an organisational plan that supports our Net Zero ambitions by identifying opportunities for sustainable technologies, buildings and operations, reducing our carbon footprint and supporting the local ecology.
This work will redefine the role of our museum and gallery in a changing cultural landscape; strengthening partnerships, rebuilding trust, and ensuring the long-term sustainability of the organisation."

"In 2017 we successfully completed Phase 1 of the major works to ensure the continued use of All Saints Church, Snodland. We are now preparing for Phase 2, the repair of the rainwater goods and falling masonry. These are currently failing and causing deterioration to the historic Kentish ragstone. The repairs will stop further damage to the building which is causing the building to be at risk and see the church in good condition.

Our activity programme follows on from the first phase, building on the existing relationships with local schools and uniformed groups, historical societies and wildlife groups. We will build new connections and reach new audiences, expanding what we can do, how we share our heritage, and what we can offer our visitors. This includes incorporating new digital elements to interpretation and increasing the use and biodiversity of our churchyard."

column2: "The Jules Anneessens Organ Restoration, Sacred Heart Church, Redcar"
column3:
"Our vision is very simple.  We want to restore to full working order the uniquely designed 1923 Jules Anneessens organ and train the next generation of organists.  We want to share the heritage and the story of our wonderful organ and organ music with our community in the church, in the town and in the region.
Our church is a community of people.  We intend that the project will support our vision which is of a thriving community, contributing to the wider community to build a more sustainable, more just and more environmentally mindful world.  Pope Francis set this out beautifully https://www.vatican.va/content/francesco/en/encyclicals/documents/papa-francesco_20150524_enciclica-laudato-si.html
and Pope Leo similarly https://www.ehn.org/pope-leo-signals-strong-support-for-climate-action-and-environmental-care

We value our heritage in Redcar and the organ restoration matters to people here.  The organ is essential to our church and its restoration will be a major contribution to the achievement of our broader vision."

column2: "Yiddishkeit, Discovering and Collecting Songs and Stories from a Lost World."
column3: "Yiddishkeit, Discovering and Collecting Stories from a Lost World. We want to deliver an oral history and cultural project based on the recollections of Holocaust Survivors, Second and Third Generation families to discover and identify what Yiddishkeit influences from a lost Eastern European Ashkenazi have been handed on. January 2026 is the eightieth anniversary of the date that the last of the 300 Ashkenazi Jewish child Holocaust survivors who had come to the Lake District in August 1945 actually departed the Lakes to continue their journey of recovery. Yiddishkeit is a term that can refer broadly to Judaism or specifically to forms of Orthodox Judaism when used particularly by religious and Orthodox Ashkenazi from roots in Eastern Europe. In a more general sense, it has come to mean the "Jewishness" or "Jewish essence" of Ashkenazi Jews in general and the traditional Yiddish-speaking Jews of Eastern and Central Europe in particular."

"Through this project, Local Services 2 You (LS2Y) aims to preserve and celebrate the untold history of Deighton Carnival—an iconic cultural event rooted in Caribbean traditions, resilience, and community pride. As we approach its 25th anniversary in 2026, our vison is to see this underrepresented community’s voices and traditions captured for future generations."

column2: "A Pick, The Pike and A Pear Tree"
column3:
"We will transform St Cuthbert’s Church from a vulnerable building into a vibrant, resilient community landmark, safeguarding over a thousand years of worship, craft, and memory while fostering inclusive connection, learning, and wellbeing in one of England’s most remote rural parishes.

The surrounding upland fells, often misread as empty, hold a dense weave of cultural and ecological histories shaped by miners, farmers, and quarry-workers. We will reveal these intertwined narratives through community-led interpretation: heritage walks from a dry-stone gathering point, seasonal activities in the graveyard meadow, storytelling rooted in local voices, and events that bring past and present into dialogue.

In a place where isolation is common and communal spaces rare, this project will upgrade and secure St Cuthbert’s future as a living place of heritage and community, rooted in the land and defined by enduring stewardship to become a vital hub for creativity, connection, care, and cultural exchange."

column2: "The National Centre for Folk and Fable - Connecting Cultural Chronicles - the stories that bring us together in a world that often sets us apart"
column3:
"Better understanding of community connections/values to inform plans for transitioning to the national centre for folk and fables, helping to secure this building's future, ensuring its rich heritage at its core. 

Our beating heritage heart: Discover, celebrate, protect heritage stories of communities' interactions and emotional connections with this newly reimagined, repurposed building. Captured by trained/supported children/young people (Grimmvestigators/Story Sleuths) its future custodians. Intergenerational project that reignites excitement and value, connecting intangible heritage with the fabric of this important heritage site. 

Living connections with culture and heritage become principal feature of Rotherham’s annual Festival of Stories: launching 2026 as legacy of Rotherham’s festival year, celebrating becoming world’s first Children’s Capital of Culture, a whole town movement initiated by Grimm & Co. 

Connect communities/bridge the divide: Illuminate/animate stories of social practices/sharing/rituals/ceremonies/festivities across cultures to recognise and raise awareness of commonalities, build appreciation, celebrate diversity together, imaginatively share with +12,000 people across Yorkshire."

"MountMove CIC wants to reconnect Sheffield’s younger generation with their roots while equipping them with skills for the future. Too many young people in the city feel disconnected from its proud industrial and working-class heritage, while also facing barriers to employment. ESS will tackle both issues together. Over 12 weeks, 30–60 young adults aged 18–30 will take part in workshops that blend employability and digital skills with local heritage exploration. They will develop confidence in communication, negotiation, teamwork and digital tools, while recording and sharing oral histories from older Sheffield residents. These stories – covering the steel industry, migration, resilience and community life – will be turned into podcasts, blogs and videos, shared online and preserved in Sheffield Archives. By the end, participants will have new skills, stronger pride in their city and an understanding of how their community’s past connects to their own future."

column2: "Sherwood’s Living Legends – Conserving the Ancient and Veteran Trees of Sherwood Forest"
column3:
"The ancient and veteran trees (AVTs) of Sherwood Forest could all be lost before the end of this century. Sherwood’s Living Legends will secure the long-term survival and continuity of Sherwood’s AVTs by creating a resilient, well-connected landscape that integrates ecological conservation, cultural heritage, and inclusive community engagement. Sherwood will be transformed into a national exemplar of tree heritage protection by systematically identifying and conserving AVTs, empowering landowners and professionals with the skills and knowledge to manage them, and reconnecting people with this iconic landscape.
Fostering a deep-rooted sense of place and stewardship, will ensure that Sherwood’s AVTs are not only preserved as vital habitats for rare and specialist species, but also cherished as cultural symbols that inspire pride, creativity, and connection. Through innovative conservation practices, inclusive programming, and sector-wide knowledge sharing, we will build a legacy of environmental excellence and community resilience that endures for generations to come."
column11: National Lottery Heritage Grants £250,000 to £10 million

column3:
"Woodlouse or slater? Cheesy bug or chucky pig? Whichever you choose, your dialect is more than words: it is rooted in where you come from, work and live.  
Our project will enhance people’s sense of belonging and connection to each other and the places important to them, by promoting understanding of this priceless, ‘at risk’ intangible heritage that we carry within us. 
With partners across the country, our ambitious programme – including events, exhibitions, creative activities, volunteering and an interactive website – will enable people (particularly those who feel socially or physically isolated) to take part in (and do!) dialect research, saving and sharing their heritage in ways that are fun, engaging and meaningful. 
We will stimulate intergenerational conversations, foster interaction between urban and rural communities, promote wellbeing, and embed skills and resilience in the heritage sector to leave a lasting legacy for everyone: individuals, Lottery players, our partners and their communities."
column11: National Lottery Heritage Grants £250,000 to £10 million

column2: "The Music of Life: celebrating the 70th anniversary of pioneering music therapy at The Horton Epsom (TMOL)"
column3:
"The Music Of Life (TMOL) project is the next significant step in the strategic development of our organisation in becoming an important destination for people in Surrey to experience heritage. It builds on the success of our NLHF-funded capital renovation project and the operational growth we have achieved since opening the building to the public three years ago. 
In-depth research and an exciting, relevant public engagement programme will strengthen our relationships with key regional stakeholders and attract new audiences to explore diversified aspects of our tangible and intangible heritage, both physically and digitally, and to contribute their own stories. 
TMOL will secure expertise and the capacity to develop new skills and heritage stories that will support our organisation and its infrastructure in a long-term sustainable future."
column14: Horton Chapel Arts And Heritage Society

column2: "A radical approach to crafting the future of The Peace Museum"
column3:
"This transformational project will secure the future of the UK’s only museum dedicated to peace. Our relocation to Salts Mill has revealed both the power and vulnerability of our heritage: visitor numbers have grown exponentially, yet rising costs are not adequately reflected in our income. It is now imperative that the organisation itself must evolve to meet new demand.

This project will strengthen the Museum’s foundations, creating a financially resilient, well-governed and environmentally responsible organisation that can sustain and share its unique heritage for the long term. We will define a clear mission, embed value-led practice across all we do, and develop the tools and skills needed to diversify income and reach new audiences.

In doing so, we will safeguard stories at risk being lost, ensuring they continue to inspire change. The Peace Museum will emerge stronger, more sustainable, and central to Bradford’s cultural legacy beyond 2025."

column2: "Pride, Passion and Skills - Made in Sheffield"
column3:
"The project aims to preserve Sheffield’s rich heritage of toolmaking and cutlery through digitisation, co-creation, and outreach, and by working closely with traditional manufacturing companies to support them to value and retain traditional skills and processes. 

It will save heritage by capturing people’s experiences and manufacturing processes before they are lost. Through digital catalogues, films, and interactive exhibitions, the Trust will ensure Sheffield’s manufacturing legacy remains relevant, accessible, and resilient for future generations.


Inclusion, participation, and knowledge exchange are central, with activities for young people, company employees and their families, and for people in our more challenged communities around the museum. Co-creation will develop skills and engage people with the heritage. 


We will support environmental sustainability by showcasing sustainability in heritage manufacturing methods, promoting recycling, and by encouraging sustainable practices among volunteers and partners. 


Our organisational sustainability will be strengthened through governance reviews, volunteer recruitment, and through digital infrastructure upgrades."

"Coal mining employed millions, but our Museum is now the very last surviving deep colliery in England. It is a critical time for our Museum and what is an extraordinarily important heritage. This project will give England's last miners and their families the chance to shape its future. /// With partners, we'll organise nationwide workshops, public events, a 'Coalfield Assembly' and online reflections platform. /// A major publication and creative digital commissions will record how coalfield communities understand that heritage and drive how we share stories into the future. // Engagement across communities in Yorkshire will shape how we connect and engage audiences. /// Digital interventions co-designed with England's last miners will boost the authenticity of our underground visitor experience. A new network will support heritage partners nationwide. // Our project will have a profound impact for our museum and for coal mining heritage nationally, transforming that heritage for ever."
column14: National Coal Mining Museum For England Trust Ltd

column2: "Tenacious by Nature: Creating a ‘Greenprint’ for Yorkshire Wildlife Trust’s Flagship Nature Reserves and their Nature Discovery Centres."
column3:
"Marking our 80th anniversary, 2026 is a pivotal year for Yorkshire Wildlife Trust. Building on the insights of our State of Yorkshire’s Nature Report (2024), the bold ambition of our Bringing Yorkshire’s Nature Back Blueprint (2025), and the direction of our new Charitable Strategy (2025-2030), we embark on this milestone year with renewed hope, determination and purpose. We now need to harness this momentum, along with our expertise, assets and networks, to drive forward nature’s recovery across Yorkshire. 

At the heart of this ambition are our four Flagship Nature Reserves and their Nature Discovery Centres, which have enormous potential to become leading beacons of nature recovery, community connection and financial resilience. Through this project we will create a ‘Greenprint’ that sets out how we can build a culture of organisational tenacity and transform these key sites into financially generative, community-aligned assets that deepen our impact for both wildlife and people."

column2: "Exploring industrial and natural heritage in north Nottinghamshire through creative practice"
column3: "Working with 10 young people (YP) aged 16-19 attending REAL Education, an alternative provision (AP), engaging them with local history through exploration of the conflicting role of mining and natural heritage in Nottinghamshire through field research, creative practices, and co-creation of a visual book. Students will learn about the role of archival images and visual culture in our lives through generations, examining the use of photography for sharing histories and visual knowledge to increase understanding of preservation and documentation of heritage. Working with heritage professionals and creative practitioners, students will have high-quality learning experiences and outcomes, increasing the connection and pride with the heritage of their local area through facilitating discussion on the impact of the mining industry in Nottinghamshire in terms of society, economy, nature, class. The coproduction and distribution of the accessible visual book will provide greater awareness of local heritage to more audiences outside of the project."

"Our vision is a Sussex rich in wildlife, valued and protected by everyone, informed by direct consultation and dialogue with our membership (38,000+), reserve visitors, community groups and partners. By 2030 we have achievable ambitions including: restore and protect 30% of land and sea for nature, inspire 1 in 4 people to take meaningful action for wildlife and build a stronger, more inclusive and diverse movement. But success relies on everyone being able to take part. Through this project, physical and social barriers to enjoying and accessing nature will be overcome, enabling people from all communities, backgrounds, and lived experiences to feel welcome, valued, and empowered.
