column14: Bath and North East Somerset Council

column2: "Realising the potential of the Conflict & Legacy Interpretive Network"
column3: "This application is being made on behalf of the Conflict and Legacy Interpretive Network, which aims to connect museums and heritage organisations actively engaged in conflict and legacy issues. The primary objective of the network is to promote, acknowledge and respect different perspectives on the recent conflict in and about Northern Ireland, commonly known as 'the Troubles'. To date, the network has focused on relationship building and developing a new website, https://conflictlegacy.org, which serves as a central resource. This initial phase was enabled by the Esmée Fairburn Collections Fund (now concluded). The proposed project aims to strengthen and consolidate the network through the appointment of a three-year Project Coordinator position.  A programme budget has also been built into this application to further support relationship building and to widen and deepen the scope of engagement, with the aim of becoming an exemplar for open and ethical dialogue around contested history."
column14: National Museums and Galleries of Northern Ireland

column2: "St Augustine's Church of Ireland - Sexton’s Cottage – Keystone for Preservation, Accessibility and Sustainability"
column3:
"The applicant is St Augustine's Church of Ireland.

The proposal relates to the preservation & renovation of the historic Sexton’s Cottage (listing reference HB01/19/012B). The cottage is a four-bay storey-and-a-half rendered vernacular dwelling, built c.1834 and situated on the edge of the historically sacred site of St. Augustine's, recognised as the former site of St. Columba's original monastery. The Sexton’s Cottage has fallen into a state of disrepair and is no longer used as a church asset. There is a critical risk of loss of this important heritage.

The renovated Sexton’s Cottage will be remodelled as a high quality heritage & tourism accommodation venue attracting visitors from throughout the world to this historic area. This initiative will be the keystone to the long-term sustainability of St Augustine's Church historic site through generating recurrent income to support activities & accessibility and facilitating continuous reinvestment in the fabric of the wider venue."

column2: "#HP Grimsby Print Heritage Project - Making a Good Impression"
column3:
"What If We Create CIC will revive and celebrate Grimsby’s rich history of printmaking by highlighting the technical and artistic skills of the town's past workforce. The project will preserve the social and industrial history of the period, ensuring this heritage is not forgotten. 

Living heritage space where the public can explore Grimsby’s printmaking legacy. 

Create opportunities for volunteers to learn and share endangered letterpress printmaking. 

Collaboration with local creatives to develop workshops that bring the town's printmaking history to life, to inspire new audiences. 

Community engagement through a program of workshops, ensuring the knowledge of traditional printmaking techniques is passed on to future generations. 

The project will not only preserve Grimsby's historical contributions to printmaking but also build a bridge to the future by fostering creativity and improving community spirit. It will provide a sustainable model for heritage preservation while inspiring a new generation of artists and makers."

"Dom Polski’s Coming of Age project will explore and document the migration stories of Polish and other ethnic minority communities in Northern Ireland, focusing on North Belfast. This is a vital first step toward our longer-term goal ambition to restore Somerton House, a Grade B listed building—being granted to us on a long lease by the Down and Connor Diocesan Trust—into a Polish House: a vibrant, multicultural hub for culture, heritage, and community life. Through storytelling, participatory research, and cultural events, the project will explore the idea of “home” across generations and cultures, engaging both first-generation migrants and second-generation youth who are growing up with blended identities. Informed by the #PL20NI project, delivered by For Your Freedom & Ours CIC,  we will use storytelling and community events to reflect on the meaning of “home” and engage people in shaping a shared space for cultural identity and inclusion."

column2: "The Most Tiresome Place in the World: Jane Austen and Bath"
column3: "Jane Austen hated the City of Bath. Well, she didn’t exactly hate it, but she certainly didn’t love it. In 2025 we celebrate the 250th anniversary of Jane Austen's birth, a unique opportunity to explore the complicated relationship she had with Bath at one of its most famous buildings, No.1 Royal Crescent.  In a year when many events in the UK will mark this important anniversary, we want to look through a different lens, and explore why Austen disliked the city that is now an indivisible part of the Austen 'brand'. Using letters, contemporary responses and borrowing the only manuscript she ever wrote in Bath, an exhibition, a writer in residence and learning activities, will reveal the highs and lows of Austen's time in the City. Creating a legacy of looking beyond the comfortable costume dramas to see how turbulence and loss cast a long shadow over Austen and Bath."

column2: "From Past to Present: The Restoration of St. Paul’s Church"
column3:
"The From Past to Present: The Restoration of St. Paul’s Church project will safeguard and revitalise St. Paul’s Church in Garvagh, ensuring it remains a functional place of worship, a centre for heritage engagement, and a vital community space for future generations.

Our objectives are threefold:

Heritage Conservation:
Carry out urgent restoration work to prevent further structural deterioration of this Grade B2 listed building.
Address key issues such as water ingress, dry rot, inadequate ventilation, and outdated heating/electrical systems.
Ensure all restoration works align with best conservation practices while preserving the building’s architectural and historical integrity.

Heritage Engagement & Education:
Develop and deliver an activity program to make local heritage more accessible and interactive for a diverse audience.
Implement guided tours, workshops, exhibitions, digital storytelling, and heritage interpretation to engage the community.
Collaborate with schools, local history groups, and cultural organisations to create educational opportunities centred on St. Paul’s Church and the wider history of Garvagh.

Community Inclusion & Sustainability:
Improve accessibility by making the church more welcoming and functional for all visitors, including those with mobility challenges.
Develop a long-term maintenance plan and build capacity within the community to ensure sustainable management of the church beyond the project's lifespan.
Strengthen partnerships with heritage organisations, conservation experts, and local stakeholders to support the church’s ongoing role in the community.

Through these objectives, we will not only preserve a historic building but also transform St. Paul’s into a living heritage hub, celebrating the cultural and historical significance of Garvagh."
column11: National Lottery Heritage Grants £250,000 to £10 million

column3:
"Inner City Trust (the Trust) will breathe new life into the former Austins Department Store (Austins) as a sustainable and engaging public library and education centre. Our vision is to:
•	Rescue this iconic and significant heritage building from terminal decay and decline and to preserve it for the future.
•	Restore Austins to its former civic prominence and revive its catalytic importance in the rebirth of the city centre.
•	Reimagine its future as a vibrant, sustainable and accessible new use for wide public benefit.
At the very heart of our vision is a desire, through heritage regeneration, to support communities and foster a love for learning, personal growth, and human connection. The Trust will deliver this vision and ensure Austins is held in the long term for the benefit of the city and current and future generations."
column11: National Lottery Heritage Grants £250,000 to £10 million

column2: "“Restoring a Shared Past: The O’Neill Chalice and Our Franciscan Story”"
column3: "The O’Neill Chalice is a rare 17th-century Franciscan liturgical object from the time of religious suppression in Ireland. Its hand-inscribed base links it directly to Fr Paul O’Neill (Guardian, 1629) and the convent at Carrickfergus. Despite its significance, the chalice has not been conserved and is at risk of further deterioration due to metal corrosion and historic damage. The heritage it represents—hidden, persecuted faith—is not currently interpreted for the public. Its story, discovered and researched through parish and historical sources, has the potential to inspire local schools, historians, and community groups. There is also an opportunity to reclaim an overgrown area between the church and primary school to create a heritage garden, linking nature with Franciscan spirituality and enhancing public access and learning."

column2: "Our Hidden Healers - the untold heritage beyond the walls"
column3: "Exploring the house’s 250-year history, we will focus on a powerful but underrepresented and untold narrative of the women and the medical legacies associated with this site.   In this project we want to explore and discover the role of women as hidden healers, celebrating the untold medical and social heritage of St. Columb’s Park House in Derry/Londonderry.  We will explore the connection to this house of the medical, nursing and caring professions including during the war effort through to the more modern day, (1985 when the Hospital Authority terminated health provision at St Columb's), championing the role women played in delivering health care provision in the Waterside area over that 45 year period.   This initiative will engage the local community in unearthing and celebrating forgotten stories, re-animating spaces of healing, and inspiring new generations through heritage-based learning."

"RHP  wishes to build on its very successful Living History Project. we  modernised  the exhibition at the Cardinal Ó Fiaich Heritage centre creating  heritage hub, created  awareness of  local archaeological sites. 

This project has been a catalyst for opening dialogue  among  local and wider community on the need to preserve the rich heritage and culture we have.

Building on this momentum. We  now want to create a strong framework for rural heritage, and traditions  to thrive sustainably in South Armagh.  As well as the archaeological sites, the area has a range of unique rich heritage features, like barrows, mounds, pillar stones, ancient trackways, ramparts, and field boundaries

Therefore we want to support the wider rural community, local farm families and individuals, to have a better understanding of the importance off and  how to maintain /sustain these sites and features and the  associated heritage, crafts and farming traditions of this area."

column2: "The Glebe Kilclief – a Green Community Hub for People, Plants & Pollinators"
column3: "Through this project HCT aims to engage with its local communities in transforming its 8.5-acre Glebe House estate into a sustainable Green Community Hub, increasing environmental diversity and growing food in a nature-friendly way.  Our vision is to achieve the conservation of our site’s fragile and ecologically rich environment, uncover and share its historical and cultural heritage, and build a long-term community-led model of stewardship and environmental education. By harnessing our rich social and environmental heritage resources through the process of creating a Land Use Map, Conservation Management Plan and associated Action Plan  we aim to address social and environmental challenges including rural isolation and well-being. The legacy from this Phase 1 Project is to lay the foundations for future, larger-scale activities to develop HCT's vision of a welcoming space for all which aligns too with NLHF’s priorities of heritage conservation, environmental protection, community engagement, inclusion and organisational sustainability."

"Through this project we would like the heritage of the Linen Industry in the Bannside area of Ballymena, with a specific focus on Frazer & Haughton, Hillmount, Cullybackey, to be understood and the extreme importance this industry had for this area.  We will be improving the understanding of the linen industry by an oral history project with those connected to the factory, collecting and recording this and other memorabilia and ensuring the information is shared as widely as possible to all. We will also work with the Frazer family to preserve surplus material from the original factory to use to demonstrate the linen process and turn the material into new products.  This will be done through working with Arthur Cottage (demonstrations) and sewing classes to produce products for use in planned exhibitions."

"Test Card - History of British television seen through a diverse lens. Forgotten and under-acknowledged people of colour (POC) have impacted British heritage through television on and off screen. As the end of the terrestrial era draws close Oral histories will be captured before they are lost forever. Historical accuracy is assured through partnerships with Channel 4, BFI, Creative Diversity network, Directors UK, Rising Waves and Film and TV Charity.
Heritage is strengthened through digital and in person work sharing 30 portraits and 15 first person podcasts, stored on MoC’s accessible digital museum. Heritage is shared through three intergenerational topical discussions, the narrative that accompanies the portraits and a co-created quiz.
Organisational resilience is built by digital up-skilling, increasing capacity and embracing sustainability. Contributing to the UK’s national heritage story of community cohesion by uncovering undocumented contributions and restoring forgotten representations of our rich cultural diversity to the public eye."

"Community Rhythms will document, preserve and celebrate the rich spoken word and musical traditions of Bristol’s Somali and East African diaspora by creating and sharing a lasting archive of music and sound that explores themes of motherhood, family dynamics and migration.

Community Rhythms is a community-led programme that will create safe, inclusive and joyful spaces for women and their families to share these histories and traditions and evolving cultural practices and strengthen bonds across the community and across generations. 

Rooted in the findings of a recent partnership participatory research initiative, Community Rhythms responds to community-identified concerns of cultural loss, familial and community isolation and challenges of culturally sensitive participation.

Community Rhythms' activities includes creative workshops (eg Women's Circles), capacity building (eg, community facilitation training) and the creation of a new Narrative Soundscape to share and archive the sounds and music that tell the story of East African families in Bristol."

"Our ambition is to expand upon the successful Townscape Heritage Programme Cleethorpes 2018-2025 and provide a seamless transition to amplify Levelling Up Fund investment in the resort with this new project.  Cleethorpes Heritage Revealed will build the heritage led evidence base for Cleethorpes, including revision of the Cleethorpes Central Seafront Conservation Area Assessment (CCSCAA) 2016 leading to larger applications for heritage regeneration.  This will:
-	Enhance heritage buildings in Cleethorpes delivering the ambitions within Cleethorpes Masterplan
-	Create stronger civic pride and sense of belonging, delivering the ambitions of NEL’s Heritage Place programme
-	Bring vacant floorspace back into use, especially upper floors to support communities
-	Engage with property owners, residents, stakeholders and visitors who value, appreciate and understand their heritage
-	Build effective trusted partnership working between freeholders/tenants and public sector
-	Strengthen resilience and build capacity to develop and lead place-based heritage partnerships.
-	Enhance digital accessibility."

"In Your Space Circus (IYSC) is restoring the historic Cathedral School in Derry-Londonderry, transforming it into a vibrant home for circus, creativity and inclusive heritage. Phase 2 will save the Grade B+ listed building, currently on the Heritage at Risk Register, through essential restoration and upgrades, creating a community hub for circus training, performance and heritage engagement.
A five-year Heritage Activity Plan will bring the site’s story to life through creative tours, workshops, oral histories and performances, celebrating both the school’s past and the rich, underexplored history of circus in Northern Ireland.
The restored building will enable IYSC to expand its work with communities and become heritage makers, embedding heritage across everything it does. Developed through extensive consultation, the project offers wide-reaching cultural, educational and social benefits. The Cathedral School will be a place where heritage is remembered, lived, active, joyful and shared together."
column11: National Lottery Heritage Grants £250,000 to £10 million

column3:
"The Mourne Gullion Landscape Connections project unites partners, farmers, landowners & communities across 73,294ha in 2 Areas of Outstanding Natural Beauty to address the root causes of an iconic landscape under significant pressure. Escalating challenges across the landscape – devastating wildfires, agricultural & land use pollution, uncoordinated land management & growth of recreational use - are contributing to a deepening environmental crisis. 

Through a depth & breadth of quality engagement & collaboration, the project will build on the knowledge and skills among those who live, work and visit this landscape to restore the connection between people and place. It will catalyse the societal, community and individual shifts needed to drive systemic change and support the landscape’s recovery and climate resilience. Modelling best practice, the project will help restore habitats, demonstrate a pathway for sustainable landscape management, enhance accessibility and restore meaningful connections to the rich and diverse natural and cultural heritage."
column14: The National Trust For Places Of Historic Interest Or Natural Beauty

column2: "#HP Window to 1913: Restoring 9-29 Victoria Street, Grimsby"
column3:
"Our ambition is to deliver an iconic heritage-led regeneration scheme at the Former House of Fraser (FHOF) department store in the heart of Grimsby’s Central Conservation Area.  It will expand upon the successful Heritage Action Zone, amplify Levelling Up Fund investment and create the foundations for future heritage investment in Grimsby, a Heritage Place. 

Through the project, we will:
•	Better understand the architectural, historical and social value of the FHOF building to share with stakeholders and the community
•	Replace the 1970s shopfront with one inspired by the 1920s Guy & Smith shopfront.
•	Explore and celebrate the heritage of the FHOF building, and Victoria Street, through the delivery of an engaging participatory programme of events and activities
•	Generate interest and support in a future area-based scheme for Grimsby
•	Maintain benefits and outcomes through webpages, continued engagement with community groups and stakeholders, and activation of the building by new tenants"

column2: "#HP Heritage Channel - broadcasting NEL’s diverse heritage"
column3:
"‘The Heritage Channel – broadcasting NEL’s diverse heritage’ will evolve our successful digital heritage platform to engage new audiences, amplify unheard voices and support the preservation of North East Lincolnshire’s (NEL’s) cultural heritage. We will develop new digital content, train underrepresented groups to tell their own heritage stories and use live streaming to increase engagement.

This project will diversify participation in heritage, strengthen our partnerships with local heritage organisations, and build the skills and confidence of people and communities through training and mentoring in heritage production and broadcasting. 

The legacy of this project will be a rich, inclusive video archive of local heritage, a digitally strong and connected local heritage sector, and a resilient Heritage Channel media platform ready to support place-based and strategic work in the area. Embedded within the Heritage Place initiative, this will support the wider ambition to improve NEL’s sense of place and its heritage value."

column2: "Recording and Sharing the Heritage of Loughinisland"
column3:
"Through this project, we want to record, preserve and share the history and stories of the Loughinisland area before they are lost. Many older residents hold knowledge that has never been written down or recorded, and there is no central place where the area’s heritage is documented or made accessible.

By gathering oral histories, carrying out a heritage audit and creating a digital archive, we aim to protect local memory, strengthen community pride and make the area’s heritage easier to understand and celebrate. The project will also bring people together across generations and give volunteers new skills through training and involvement in delivery.
We want this work to create a foundation for future heritage activity and ensure the story of Loughinisland is available to schools, local people, and the wider public for years to come."

column2: "From Flood to Future: Preserving Downpatrick Railway’s historical heritage Bridges"
column3:
"This project will protect and restore a rare and historically significant surviving section of the former Belfast & County Down Railway, safeguarding four bridges recorded on the Historic Environment Record of Northern Ireland. Without urgent intervention, their accelerated deterioration following the extreme weather of 2023 risks irreversible loss. Restoration will maintain public access to the Loop Platform, Inch Abbey and the wider heritage landscape, ensuring continued operation of the Downpatrick & County Down Railway as a valued community, tourism and educational asset.

Alongside capital repairs, the project will deliver a flood-awareness and infrastructure lifecycle initiative for local schools through curriculum-linked activities. Pupils will explore why Downpatrick floods, how bridges are engineered to withstand extreme weather, and how climate resilience is built into heritage conservation, an especially relevant issue for the town. Volunteers will also receive structured working-over-water awareness training. Together, these measures protect heritage, build resilience and reinforce long-term sustainability."
column14: Downpatrick and County Down Railway Society Limited

column2: "The Middle Glens: Our Heritage, Our Future."
column3:
"The Old Church Centre opened in 2019 to provide a dedicated Heritage, Arts, and Community space for Cushendun and the wider area. It has exceeded all expectations hosting a varied programme of over 140 events in the last two years alone, all volunteer led. 

Heritage has always been at the forefront of our vision, and this project will enable us to do so much more to identify, document and showcase the story of the Mid-Glens.  A dedicated heritage officer will support us in creating a lasting and accessible heritage resource bank, expanded digital and physical archives, and strengthened community engagement and long-term partnerships. The Old Church Centre will become firmly established as the area’s heritage hub, a place where everyone can learn about and enjoy our unique heritage for years to come."

"Lottery investment will enable local people to create a connected, climate-resilient landscape across the 90,603 ha of Strangford & Lecale AONB: a “wholescape” approach where habitats are bigger, better and more joined-up where communities lead how people and nature reconnect.

Our project is driven by three core innovations:

1. Community Clusters – local stewardship hubs co-designing best practice interventions and leaving an empowered legacy.
2. A flexible, evidence-based Library of Measures – tailored approaches to habitat restoration and heritage care that fit local land use while delivering public goods: biodiversity, clean water, carbon storage and flood mitigation.
3. A strategic Nature Recovery Network (NRN) – ensuring landscape scale, connected habitat recovery aligned with regional policy and community priorities.

We will embed systemic change in governance, land management and community practice, restoring key habitats, reviving traditional knowledge, and creating inclusive pathways for engagement, skills, volunteering and youth leadership that sustain a thriving people–nature relationship."
column14: Newry, Mourne and Down District Council

column3:
"Through this project, Tyrone Dippers aims to improve the physical and mental wellbeing of people in Strabane and the wider Derry City and Strabane District Council area by providing safe, supported access to cold-water dipping and outdoor wellbeing activities. We want to create an inclusive, welcoming space where people can connect with others, build confidence, and enjoy the benefits of nature regardless of income, background or ability. Our project will particularly support people who are educationally or economically disadvantaged, helping them access free wellbeing opportunities at a time when many households face financial pressures.

We aim to reduce isolation, strengthen community relationships and encourage positive lifestyle habits through regular dips, wellbeing sessions, environmental activities and volunteer-led support. By offering a structured, community-led programme, we hope to empower local people, promote resilience and create long-term improvements in health, confidence and community connection across the district."

"The “Foyle Flow: Our Stories, Our Rivers” project seeks to reconnect communities with the rich intangible cultural heritage linked to the rivers, burns and streams of the Foyle Catchment. While these waterways have shaped local identity, livelihoods and daily life from Neolithic times to today, much of the associated folklore, traditions and lived experience remains undocumented and at risk of being lost. 

Through a two-year, people-focused programme, Loughs Agency will deliver workshops, oral history recordings and participatory learning activities to capture and celebrate this heritage. Working collaboratively with communities, schools and heritage partners, the project will document placenames, fishing traditions, bridge histories, folklore and personal memories. By preserving and sharing these stories through exhibitions, digital outputs and educational resources, the project will safeguard this valuable heritage. It will also inspire greater community pride, awareness and long-term stewardship of the rivers for future generations."

column2: "Dolemeads at 125 years old - the first council housing in Bath"
column3:
"Dolemeads Residents Group — a sub-group of the Widcombe Association — seeks to preserve and celebrate the heritage of the Dolemeads: Bath's first council housing estate, in its 125th year. Built in 1901, this pioneering red brick estate stands apart from the city's celebrated Georgian limestone, yet its story has been  absent from Bath's historical record.
This project we will create a lasting body of heritage assets: a documentary film capturing oral histories from residents and historians; permanent entrance signage giving the estate its rightful place in Bath's story; a QR-enabled History Walk connecting past and present through archival maps, photographs and plans; and community workshops for local schoolchildren. These will culminate in the inaugural Dolemeads Day 2026 — a public celebration bringing the community together around its own history.
All outputs will be permanently archived with Bath Record Office and freely accessible online, ensuring this story endures for generations."

column2: "From the Ground Up - A Heritage Hub for NE Lincolnshire"
column3:
"January 2026, Our Big Picture (OBP) reopened our Grade 2-listed town centre venue after capital works. We look to build on our proven, responsive, place-based approach, dismantling barriers for underserved communities, uncovering and sharing hidden stories, and cultivating transformative collaborations.
Through 2025, 4,531 people participated in heritage activities, including 1,457 children and young people, who told us they want to explore heritage creatively, lead, and be heard.

With Heritage Fund support, we will invest in resources, enabling OBP to move from an emerging coordinating presence to an established Heritage Hub and deliver three community-shaped activities over 20mths.

1.	NEL Festival of Archaeology 2026/2027- community digs, artist-led workshops, Days of Discovery for schools and wider communities
2.	Medieval Grimsby- our venue is a lens into the town’s hidden past
3.	Gentle Voices: Silent Stories, NEL's first Women's Heritage Network, designed by and for members. Surfacing untold stories of women and girls."

column2: "Newry Cathedral - Protecting the Past and Embracing the Future"
column3:
"Newry Parish seeks to restore the Cathedral of St Patrick and St Colman as a sustainable heritage, tourism and community hub at the heart of a growing city facing significant socio-economic challenges. Welcoming over 200,000 visitors annually, the project will preserve the Cathedral’s historic fabric and mosaics while securing its legacy for future generations ahead of its bicentenary in 2029.
The project will strengthen Newry’s wider regeneration and tourism agenda by increasing access to heritage through school programmes, guided tours, cultural events, digital interpretation and expanded volunteering. It will support community participation, cross-community engagement and opportunities for newcomers to connect with the city’s shared heritage. Investment in traditional conservation and digital skills will help preserve specialist craftsmanship while developing new skills pathways for local people.
The Cathedral gardens will be transformed into an accessible biodiversity and wellbeing space, promoting environmental education, reflection and community use within a central urban setting"

The Manchester Prize is a landmark challenge prize that aims to drive pioneering AI innovation by rewarding UK-led breakthroughs in AI for public good.The Round 2 focuses on using AI for Clean Energy Systems. The grants, managed via our delivery partner Nesta, will incentivise development of cutting-edge applications of AI to solve challenges across high-impact domains. The project aims to accelerate and showcase the potential of AI to be used in a way that benefits people, society and supports a community of leading AI for public good innovators in the UK. We anticipate that the project supports the UK governments wider objectives in the following ways:Positioning the UK as a Science and Tech Superpower: The Manchester Prize will accelerate innovation, stimulate investment and help to position the UK as a global leader in AI, supporting the AI Strategy ambition for the UK to cement its position as a science and technology superpower.Stimulating and demonstrating the use of AI for public good, in line with objective 5 of the AI Safety Summit. Solutions developed through the Manchester Prize will showcase socially beneficial UK AI innovation, as the focus of the prize challenge will be AI for Public Good and AI safety and ethics will remain a key judging criterion for the Manchester Prize. The solutions developed by finalist teams will serve as clear examples of the positive potential of AI.Supporting better outcomes for UK Citizens: By incentivising AI development in areas of public importance, like Climate Change, Energy and Environment, the prize aims to generate downstream benefits for UK society. The first round of the Prize has already accelerated the development of key AI solutions relating to areas relating topublic good areas such as energy efficiency, improving public infrastructure, reducing water loss and crop efficiency.Developing a highly skilled community of AI Innovators: The prize will contribute to nurturing the UKs world-leading AI research community, by incentivizing AI development in areas of public importance and bringing together developers, problem-holders, adopters and investors.The challenge is also closely aligned with the government's key missions, in particular, mission 1 (kickstart economic growth) through supporting investment and growth in UK technology startups and organisation and mission 2 (make Britain a clean energy superpower) through its focus on green growth and AI for clean energy systems.

column2: Gathering information for citizen science monitoring of polluting wrecks
column3: This data gathering project will create a framework for a potentially polluting wrecks (PPW) citizen science monitoring scheme to make both the environment and water-users safer. Marine environment user groups will be visited to raise awareness of PPWs to them, and the environment. These advocacy visits will establish the current knowledge of PPWs amongst the maritime community and to assess their capacity to safely and effectively collect data. In parallel, relevant government partners will be consulted to ensure that data capture is appropriate for their management of PPWs. This scheme could be disseminated globally through NAS’s international training partners.

column2: Identification of shipwrecks along the coast of Pakistan
column3: The funding will be used to support heritage research to develop educational resources and research guides, delivering in-person workshops in London whilst also connecting virtually to volunteers and staff at MaritimEA, based in Pakistan. It will support academics, maritime archaeologists and others through further research and understanding into the identification of shipwrecks and maritime disasters around the coast of Pakistan.

column2: Investigating Colonial Port Development through the Lloyd’s Register Archive.
column3:
The Nautical Archaeology Society (NAS) will lead this project, building on its experience delivering research and training initiatives associated with the Lloyd’s Register archive. NAS will coordinate project management, administration and finances, ensuring consistency and quality across all activities. The Society has partnered with one of its longest-standing International Training Partners, the Australasian Institute for Maritime Archaeology (AIMA), and one of its newest partners, MaritimEA Research in Pakistan. Both organisations represent areas of significant potential for expanding equitable maritime heritage research in the Global South.

Traditionally, International Training Partners are supported by NAS to adapt the NAS syllabus to local conditions and heritage examples. AIMA has been running a localised version of the NAS syllabus since the 1990s and will lead regional coordination and volunteer engagement in Australia. MaritimEA Research is currently developing its own case studies for integration into the NAS syllabus and is preparing to translate entry-level course content into Urdu to widen participation.

Through this collaboration, NAS will strengthen partner capacity in archival research and digital interpretation, adding a new dimension to the International Training Partner network. AIMA and MaritimEA will recruit a team of volunteers to undertake the archival research. Through experience in current LRF funded archival projects NAS will run the archival training with the support of LRF staff.

While NAS will initially provide management oversight, this feasibility phase will support AIMA and MaritimEA in developing independent project management confidence. Subsequent phases will move toward a fully collaborative, equitable partnership, further decolonising engagement with the Lloyd’s Register archive.

column2: "Pagans, Saints and Birdmen: Revealing the hidden stories of our landscape together"
column3: "Through this project we want to engage and expose the local community, and especially people either not currently engaged with heritage or areas under-represented in our (the Craigavon Historical Society) current membership, with the landscape heritage that surrounds them, whether it be the archaeology hidden beneath the ground, overlooked monuments in the landscape, or the legendary stories set in the area. To achieve this we will organise a community archaeology dig at Kilmocholmóg, an intergenerational local history schools programme, talks, tours and workshops. The project’s timing will allow us to captilise on the current enthusiasm, interest and momentum engendered throughout the local area by our previous NLHF project (Ref: NM-22-01076). By the project’s end the CHS will be strengthened through increased awareness, membership and the forging of new partnership links; while heritage within the locality will be safeguarded through increased knowledge and interest generated during our project."

"Celebrate the heritage of Burnby Hall and the life of Katherine Stewart (1872-1949), who left a great legacy in Pocklington.

We will create work for, by, and with the community to share the unknown heritage of Burnby Hall from Katherine’s perspective and encouraging the community to preserve  her story. 

Activities: activity packs, community art installations, and a celebratory event. 

Through a collaborative approach led by industry professionals, community members will explore heritage and create materials for the future.

*Raise awareness and understanding of the heritage through creative outreach and engagement activities. 
*Build a permanent installation celebrating the life and legacy of Katherine Stewart at Burnby Hall, created by, with, and for the community of Pocklington. 
*Produce a heritage celebration day event, coinciding with the celebration of key milestones for the community including Pocklington Arts Centres 25th Year, Thunk-It Theatre’s 5th Year and Heritage Volunteers’ 10-Year Anniversaries."

"This project celebrates the rich and diverse heritage of ethnic minority communities in Armagh while recognising the shared history of Irish and Ulster Scots communities. It is essential for newcomers who want to preserve their traditions and feel a sense of belonging, offering the wider community a deeper understanding of their neighbours. By capturing oral histories, hosting cultural nights, and organising a large-scale outdoor event, we ensure that languages, customs, and migration stories are not lost but preserved, shared and valued.

Our project also promotes inclusion, access, and participation by breaking down barriers that often exclude ethnic minorities from heritage spaces. Through meaningful involvement in planning and performance, as well as cross-community excursions, we ensure equal opportunity to engage with heritage. By including Irish and Ulster Scots voices alongside newcomer communities, we build mutual respect, increase representation, and foster a more cohesive, connected and tolerant Armagh for all."

"The Beverley Minster Destinations project represents a step-change for the Minster team, seeking to recognise and deliver on the regional importance of the Minster in local identity, regional tourism and the importance to local economy. In partnership with regional and local organisations we will open up access to the regional heritage of pilgrimage to the shrine of St. John of Beverley, secure the fabric of the east end for future generations, create new opportunities for volunteering, training and engagement for new audiences, and improve the outside space around the east end to make a new, more biodiverse public space for the town. We expect the legacy will be a building which is at the heart of the region’s identity and focus, structurally in good order as part of our long-term plan, sustainably maintained and able to meet the needs of all users now and in the future."

"Our project aims to secure three years of dedicated protection for the Little Tern colony at the Lagoons SSSI in Kilnsea, one of the most successful beach-nesting sites in the United Kingdom. We seek £100,000 to fund essential wardening, monitoring, predator management, visitor engagement and scientific work that ensures the long-term viability of this vulnerable species. The project will provide continuous seasonal coverage, allowing us to record productivity, safeguard nests and respond rapidly to threats such as disturbance, predation and extreme weather.
A further £10,000 will support targeted habitat management on SBOT-owned land and the leased SSSI plot, improving nesting substrate, maintaining access infrastructure and enhancing climate resilience. Over three years, we aim to maintain high breeding success, strengthen long-term datasets, involve volunteers in specialist conservation skills and support community understanding of coastal wildlife. This investment will secure stable, effective protection for a nationally important colony."

"The St. Andrew’s Partnership Project seeks to restore and revitalise the Grade I listed St. Andrew’s Church in Lt. Massingham - a peaceful village rich in nature and history. 

As the only public building in the village, listed on Heritage England's 'at-risk register' and located near Peddar’s Way, the church has the potential to become a vibrant hub for worship, community events, and cultural activities. 

Significantly, since the theft of its lead roof in 2017, the Friends of St. Andrew’s (fosalm.org) have been fundraising to create a lasting legacy by replacing the temporary roof covering which is now leaking, though rising costs from inflation continue to outpace donations.

The vision includes installing bat boxes to protect the church interior and also features a digital media screen and interpretation boards to connect the church with local walking routes, creating a rich blend of culture, nature, and history."

"We plan to deliver a heritage access and inclusion project designed to connect people in Old Goole with their heritage and the Goole 200 celebrations as Goole Town celebrates in 2026. Old Goole is isolated from the greater town by the river and docks, carrying its own unique identity and heritage. 

We will work with Old Goole residents including young people, older people, families, refugees, dock workers and migrant communities using oral history, object handling and research, to connect generations, interpret and document the social, cultural and industrial heritage of Old Goole, from early Viking settlements, though the diversion of the river in the 1600’s to the development of the port.

We will work with residents to document and creatively interpret the research, sharing and making it accessible as a heritage parade for the residents of Old Goole, and digitally through websites and social media pages for a wider audience."

"We hope to raise sufficient funds to enable the urgently needed repair and restoration of the Tower of the Church of St. Mary the Virgin in Holme-next-the-Sea, thereby preserving this Grade 1 listed building and preventing it from falling into disrepair and possible closure.

Through the creation of a documentary and static displays of our project we will raise awareness and understanding of our village’s heritage, with the aim of attracting greater numbers of visitors to the Church and the area. The promotion of our project on social media will be specifically aimed at encouraging a younger demographic to 
become involved in our community, to safeguard our organisational sustainability. 

The legacy of our project will be the continued use of the Church for regular faith services and community events, as well as the preservation of a building of historic importance for future generations."

column2: "The Workshop @Carnegie King’s Lynn: unlocking community heritage and co-designing a future"
column3:
"We will preserve the heritage of The King’s Lynn Carnegie and its surrounding area through a programme of urgent repairs and conservation. This will allow for us to deliver meanwhile activities over the coming years whilst we prepare for a future large-scale renovation and addition project. This project will see us deliver a consultation programme with local communities to co-design the building’s future as The Workshop. 
Whilst saving the Carnegie for future generations, this project will be the launchpad to the creation of a vibrant cultural and heritage hub for King’s Lynn and the region, engaging new audiences in its rich heritage.  The Carnegie building will become more environmentally and financially sustainable, our resilience as an organisation will be enhanced and importantly, through the consultation co-design work, we will build the heritage skills and capacity of local communities, making them better equipped to make decisions relating to their heritage."

"Goole’s bicentenary is a unique chance to celebrate the town’s history. This project will engage audiences with our heritage in an accessible, memorable way.

Through a new bicentenary pantomime inspired by Charles Dickens's A Christmas Carol, alongside community engagement workshops and heritage interpretation activities, we will help residents discover more about the people, industries and events that shaped Goole over the 200 years. Using its journey through past, present and future, the show will explore key moments in Goole’s history, reflect on the town today and look to its future.

We will work with local historians, community groups and residents to gather stories and historical material to shape the script and reflect community.

The project aims to raise awareness and appreciation of Goole’s heritage, foster pride in the town and its achievements, and offer an entertaining, accessible way for people of all ages to connect with where they live."

column2: "‘Aske 500’ - Sustaining the built and natural heritage of Aughton All Saints church"
column3: "‘Aske 500’ will open up access to the unique built and natural heritage of Aughton All Saints’ church, on the edge of East Yorkshire’s Derwent Ings. Our project will explore Aughton’s place in history through its connection to Robert Aske, leader of the Tudor rebellion ‘The Pilgrimage of Grace’. We will connect Aughton to regional heritage tourism offers and audiences, create new heritage experiences and resources, whilst undertaking urgent capital works to the Tower built in his memory and conserving 12th century fabric for future generations. We will create seasonal activities which enable people to access and enjoy the distinctive birdlife of the adjacent Lower Derwent National Nature Reserve, working with new partners to enhance local biodiversity and preserve fragile ecosystems, improving churchyard drainage and management regimes. The project legacy will be a building and landscape that is more easily accessed, better managed, cared for, and enjoyed by all."

"ABC Developing Heritage will deliver the first phase of the Borough’s Heritage Strategy, establishing the foundations for a coordinated, borough-wide approach to protecting, enhancing, and celebrating heritage across Armagh City, Banbridge and Craigavon.
The project will introduce dedicated governance, staffing, and an evidence-led approach to ensure heritage is understood, valued and sustainably managed. It will strengthen the sector through the creation of a Heritage Network, capacity-building programmes, and accessible grant schemes, enabling broader participation and empowering communities to shape and care for their heritage.
A robust evidence base will inform future investment and decision-making, while targeted pilot initiatives will demonstrate practical approaches to regeneration and conservation. The project will widen participation, volunteering, and learning, embedding heritage within everyday life and local decision-making.
Overall, the project will create a lasting legacy by building a resilient, connected and culturally vibrant borough, where heritage supports community cohesion, well-being, and long-term regeneration."

column3: The Affordable Homes Programme 2021-2026 (AHP 2021-26) is a £7.4 billion investment programme providing grant funding to support the capital costs of developing affordable housing for rent or sale. AHP 2021-26 offers two routes to access funding, Continuous Market Engagement (scheme-by-scheme); and Strategic Partnerships (volume grant allocations to ambitious partners). Through the AHP 2021-26 programme, there is an emphasis on partners use of Modern Methods of Construction (MMC), the delivery of high-quality sustainable design and working closely with housebuilders who are small to medium-sized enterprises (SME).

column2: "Trinity 600: Celebrating 600 years of History with Hull Minster"
column3: "2025 is a significant year for Hull Minster, as we celebrate 600 years since the church was completed and consecrated as Holy Trinity Church in 1425. Holy Trinity has been a constant presence in the city centre for centuries, and the history of the city is written within our walls. Through the recent HLF Revival Back to Life project, Hull Minster now confidently carries the reputation of a heritage building. We want to use this 600th anniversary to celebrate the significance of Hull Minster within the city, sharing the rich history and heritage of the church widely across all generations. We will share the living heritage of music, performing arts and crafts, festivals, and social practices that we have inherited and explore how they are still celebrated today. People will be immersed in the life and traditions of their ancestors that have shaped who we are as a city today."
column14: Parochial Church Council Of The Ecclesiastical Parish Of The Most Holy And Undivided Trinity, Hull

column2: "Scene but not Heard: Uncovering HU3's Queer Heritage"
column3:
"Three Ways East's work in HU3 in Hull unearthed a body of photographs documenting the LGBTQ+ and drag performance scene in working class venues in the area, in the 1980s/90s.  As the work of at least 6 photographers (including renowned photographer Daniel Meadows), it is an important record of LGBTQ+ heritage, and working- class venues as safe spaces for those who considered themselves othered.  Currently dispersed in private collections, it is not available publicly.  We would like to change this.
Alongside the original photographers, LGBTQ+ communities, local residents, some of the original drag acts and musicians, plus contemporary artists and performers, we aim to curate, present and archive a new collection of historical photographs, oral histories, exhibitions and presentations across Hull and online.  This will make visible important hidden narratives, adding to authorised heritage discourses, and empowering LGBTQ+ and local communities to shape their local heritage."

"Middle Child will reignite Hull’s lost theatrical heritage by creating Let It Burn, a major production about the city’s original Theatre Royal, which stood on Humber Street until it burnt down in 1859, and again in 1869. This untold story will be brought to life through performance, workshops and public engagement, rooted in original materials uncovered at Hull History Centre – including 19th-century programmes, contracts and rare imagery. The production will happen in our historic venue, in a conservation area steps from the original site.

As part of this work, we’ll collaborate with residents to explore the civic legacy of East Hull’s theatre-themed street names – built between 1958 and 1961 – through creative workshops, oral histories and co-designed mural.

Combining historical research with artistic reimagining and inclusive community engagement, these stories reconnect Hull with its theatrical heritage, leaving a legacy of shared memory and accessible resources for future generations."

"Orchard Park Estate (OPE), Hull, was built in 1963 in response to slum clearances, yet it has been unfairly labelled as dangerous over time.

This project seeks to challenge that misconception by capturing the estate’s true identity and celebrating its cultural roots. We'll bring together diverse groups of residents, investigating the estate’s history from 1963-2013, encompassing the much-maligned yet much-loved tower blocks later demolished.

Working hand-in-hand with the community, we'll gather personal stories and oral histories reflecting OPE’s strong traditions and maritime heritage, tracing how many residents moved from Hull’s fishing community to the new estate. With an artistic reconstruction of the demolished blocks at its centre, our final exhibition will preserve and showcase these memories, providing a fairer reflection of OPE’s lived experience.

By recording this intangible heritage, we will build pride, bridge generations, and offer OPE's people a renewed sense of belonging within the wider story of Hull."

column2: "Sound Foundations: Strengthening the Heart of Hull Minster"
column3:
"'Sound Foundations' will strengthen Hull Minster’s role as a centre for living heritage and as a vibrant community hub for Hull. It will increase the organizational capacity of the Minster to both preserve and fortify its legacy, and increase people’s engagement with the Minster and its heritage, whether they be visitors, volunteers, choristers or congregation.

We will achieve this by investing in people: expanding the roles of the Heritage Manager, Volunteer Manager, and recruiting an Assistant Director of Music. Through developing these roles, the Minster can deliver on its programme of heritage engagement, protect and improve its historic Choral Hull program, strengthen our volunteer team, and develop detailed conservation plans for the Minster and our historic Grand Organ.

By the project’s end, Hull Minster will be better equipped to manage its future on all fronts, ensuring its continued importance to the heart of its city."
column14: Parochial Church Council Of The Ecclesiastical Parish Of The Most Holy And Undivided Trinity, Hull

column3:
"Hull is often portrayed as a struggling city with no great future and this negativity is keenly felt by local people.  Through this project, residents will learn about positive and impactful people and places related to Hull.  In doing so, they will develop pride in the city, understand its history and learn what people from Hull have contributed to the world.  To ensure engagement and make the project interesting and relatable, we will focus on social heritage.

By challenging negative stereotypes, we hope to raise aspirations, shape community identity and increase optimism for the future.  This project will be aimed at people who lack the confidence and skills to engage with history and heritage.  Through this work residents will develop transferable skills, improve their social networks and access new opportunities.  Our aim is to broaden the horizons of those who are least likely to meaningfully engage with existing heritage projects."

column2: "Hull Fishing Heritage and Migrant Cultural Food: A Culinary and Cultural Journey-Phase 1"
column3:
"Hull Fishing Heritage and Migrant Cultural Food: A Culinary and Cultural Journey- phase 1, builds on previous learning and feedback by deepening community consultation and strengthening heritage outcomes. The project will explore the intersection of Hull’s fishing legacy and migrant culinary traditions through structured oral history research led by core project staff, with local fishermen, historians, and migrant communities. Participants will actively shape the project, contributing stories, recipes, and perspectives reflecting Hull’s evolving food heritage.
Interactive cooking workshops and co-designed events, including food festivals and pop-up tastings, will directly engage diverse communities in hands-on heritage activities. Partnerships with local venues and organisations will support delivery and ensure accessibility.
All recordings and materials will be archived with local heritage partners to secure a legacy. The project will culminate in a freely accessible publication and exhibition, ensuring continued public engagement and celebrating Hull’s maritime history and multicultural identity beyond the project’s lifespan."

"Our project focuses on collecting and archiving lived experience stories of Freedom from under-represented communities in Hull including Disabled, Global Majority, Working-Class people and those affected by crime.
 
Stories of community, social justice, and freedom (of movement and speech) are in danger of being lost due to:
1.	Historic institutional preferencing of colonial narratives that tell a one-sided story of history
2.	Minority voices being considered historically unimportant in the building of Hull
3.	Port city communities are sometimes transient meaning stories are not captured 
We want to:
1.	Work with trusted community partners and storytelling experts to deliver story gathering workshops in underrepresented communities across Hull
2.	Provide opportunities for these communities to tell their stories through co-created creative interventions
3.	Preserve the stories for future generations in a publicly accessible digital archive
4.	Improve sustainability by passing on storytelling/gathering skills"

column3:
The Swan Song Project (SSP) help people facing terminal illness and bereavement create lasting legacies by transforming their memories and emotions into original songs.
Through facilitated sessions with trained songwriters, SSP reach people who may not otherwise engage with traditional therapeutic support. They work with over 70 people each year through partnerships with nine hospices. However, growing referrals and a waiting list are stretching their founder-led model. With The Fore’s funding, SSP will recruit a Director of Operations and expand their freelance songwriter team. Stronger systems, hospice partnerships and income generation will position SSP for sustainable growth, enabling them to meet rising demand and extend their impact beyond Yorkshire.

column3: When Development Finance Institutions (DFIs) and Multilateral Development Banks (MDBs) invest in infrastructure, they apply safety standards to individual projects. But if the national health and safety system in a country has gaps or limited capacity, workers remain at risk regardless. This project tests a new approach - bringing together DFIs and MDBs to jointly assess a country's occupational safety and health (OSH) system, identify gaps and agree coordinated action. Led by IOSH, the pilot will produce a replicable model to help DFIs and MDBs work more effectively together to support safer conditions for workers.
